meta.blurb: Noah lives on quick meals eaten on a bicycle, and a crowd of tiny microbes in his gut eats them too. His neighbour Ines studies microbes. She shows him how everyday food feeds them, and how much science still does not know.
meta.bible: Noah: a young bicycle courier of about twenty-eight who eats quick meals on the road and wants to understand his gut; honest, hungry and a little impatient. Ines: his neighbour, a Microbiologist at a university, who studies microbes; patient, funny, and careful to say what science does not yet know. The story runs over about six weeks in a city, in Noah's flat, Ines's laboratory and a street market. Key terms: Gut, Small intestine, Large intestine, Colon, Microbes, Bacteria, Microbiome, Fibre, Prebiotics, Probiotics, Resistant starch, Polyphenols, Fermentation, Fermented foods, Short-chain fatty acids, Butyrate, Antibiotics, Constipation, Diarrhoea, Irritable bowel syndrome, Registered dietitian. Facts: the gut is several metres long; the large intestine holds most gut microbes; by recent estimates the body holds about as many microbes as human cells; microbes ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids that feed the cells lining the colon, and they also make gas; many national guides advise about thirty grams of fibre a day for adults and most adults eat less; a large citizen-science survey found that people who ate more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied set of gut microbes than people who ate ten or fewer, which is a link and not proof; a small university trial found that ten weeks of eating more fermented foods increased the variety of gut microbes; antibiotics save lives but also disturb gut microbes, and should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them. Foods: Beans, Lentils, Oats, Barley, Brown rice, Onions, Garlic, Leeks, Bananas, Yoghurt, Kefir, Kimchi, Sauerkraut, Miso. Safety facts: add fibre slowly and drink water; see a doctor for blood in the stool, black stools, unexplained weight loss, ongoing pain or a lasting change in bowel habits; people with bowel conditions, allergies, a pregnancy, a child to feed or on medicine should ask a doctor or registered dietitian; do not cut out gluten before testing for coeliac disease; home-made fermented food needs clean jars and should be thrown away if it smells bad or grows mould. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, clear and a little funny; honest about uncertainty; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice. Cast added in the full-length book: Pavel, the calm dispatcher at Noah's courier company; Tomasz, a fellow courier and Noah's friend, who always jokes; Mara, Noah's older sister, who has a small son, Leo; Kofi, Ines's patient laboratory student; Dara, who runs a fermented-food stall at the street market; Hana, a Registered dietitian at a community clinic; Dr Ellis, a family doctor. More terms: Stomach, Saliva, Gullet, Pancreas, Liver, Gall bladder, Villi, Mucus, DNA, Nerves, Hormones, Immune system, Vitamins, Soluble fibre, Insoluble fibre, Beta-glucan, Inulin, Pectin, Wholegrain, Cholesterol, Citizen-science, Ultra-processed, Emulsifiers, Lactose, Gluten, Coeliac disease, FODMAP, Bowel screening, Pasteurised, Brine, Sweetcorn, Chickpeas, Walnuts, Chia, Flax, Hummus, Tofu, Asparagus, Prunes, Bran, Porridge, Wholemeal. Further terms and places: Prebiotic, Chicory, Jerusalem artichokes, Bifidobacteria, Hadza, Tanzania, Celeriac, Leeks, Tahini, Quinoa, Buckwheat, Rye, Watercress. Microbe, Probiotic, Fibre-rich, Kimchi. Dietitian, Dietitians, Allergy, Intolerance. Lentil, Bean, Chickpea, Onion, Garlic, Banana. Further facts used in the full-length book: a food with about six grams of fibre per hundred grams may be called high in fibre in many countries; dried red kidney beans must be soaked, drained and boiled hard for at least ten minutes; cooked rice must be cooled within an hour, kept in the fridge and eaten within a day; antibiotics work on bacteria and not viruses; severe, bloody or lasting diarrhoea needs a doctor; many countries invite adults to bowel screening; a low-FODMAP diet is short, temporary and guided by a dietitian; anyone who suspects coeliac disease is tested before cutting out gluten; alcohol is not a health food; fermented foods can be high in salt; miso is stirred in after the heat is off. In the story, Noah's plant count rises from about six a week to thirty, his fibre from about eleven grams a day to about twenty and beyond, and the six weeks end with a thirty-plant dinner. Dr Ellis is a woman; Mara is Noah's older sister; Leo is her small son.
chapters: The Wire Between Gut and Brain

beats.scene: Noah eats a quick sandwich on a bicycle at a red traffic light
beats.summary: Noah, a bicycle courier, eats quick meals on the road and wonders what they do inside him.

beats.scene: Pavel the dispatcher reads out a long list of parcels on a phone screen
beats.summary: Noah's day is a chain of deliveries from his dispatcher Pavel, with no time for a proper lunch.

beats.scene: Noah's stomach rumbles while his friend Tomasz laughs beside a bicycle stand
beats.summary: Noah's stomach is often noisy and bloated, and his fellow courier Tomasz teases him about it.

beats.scene: Noah carries his bicycle upstairs while Ines unlocks her door
beats.summary: In the stairwell Noah meets his neighbour Ines, who is carrying a bag full of beans and vegetables.

beats.scene: Noah asks Ines what happens to a sandwich after he swallows it
beats.summary: Noah asks Ines what really happens inside him after a sandwich, and she says he is asking about a crowd.

beats.scene: Ines holds up a finger beside a pot of basil on her doorstep
beats.summary: Ines offers him a deal: six weeks of curiosity, small changes and honest answers, including the words I do not know.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines walk along a university corridor lined with glass doors
beats.summary: On Saturday morning Noah visits the university laboratory where Ines works.

beats.scene: Kofi smiles beside a laboratory bench with a microscope and a pot of yoghurt
beats.summary: Ines's student Kofi shows Noah living microbes in a drop of plain yoghurt under a microscope.

beats.scene: Ines gives Noah a small green notebook across a cluttered desk
beats.summary: Ines gives Noah a notebook and three rules for the six weeks: be curious, be careful, be kind to your gut.

beats.scene: Noah writes his first question in the notebook on a bench outside the university
beats.summary: Noah writes his first question in the notebook, and the story of the six weeks begins.

beats.scene: Ines draws a long winding tube on a whiteboard with a marker
beats.summary: The gut is a long tube, several metres in length, running from the mouth to the end of the body.

beats.scene: Noah chews a plain cracker at a kitchen table while Ines holds a stopwatch
beats.summary: Chewing and saliva begin digestion, and a cracker chewed for long enough starts to taste sweet.

beats.scene: Ines traces a finger down a drawing of the throat
beats.summary: Muscles in the throat and gullet squeeze food downwards, so swallowing works even upside down.

beats.scene: Ines draws a stomach like a small bag full of acid
beats.summary: The stomach churns food with strong acid, which kills many microbes that arrive with it, and holds it for a few hours.

beats.scene: Ines unrolls a paper tube with tiny folds drawn inside
beats.summary: Most food is broken down and taken into the blood in the small intestine, whose folds give it a huge surface.

beats.scene: Ines draws a liver and a pancreas beside the tube
beats.summary: The liver, the gall bladder and the pancreas send bile and juices into the small intestine to help with digestion.

beats.scene: Ines draws a thick arrow carrying leftovers out of the small intestine
beats.summary: Some food, mostly fibre, cannot be digested by human juices and travels on to the large intestine.

beats.scene: Ines draws a wide curved tube framing the small intestine
beats.summary: The large intestine is wider and shorter than the small one; it takes back water and holds most of the gut's microbes.

beats.scene: Noah eats sweetcorn beside a clock showing the time of day
beats.summary: Food takes around a day or two to travel through the gut, and the shells of sweetcorn show how fibre passes through.

beats.scene: Ines taps a thin line along the wall of her drawing
beats.summary: The inside of the gut is in a sense outside the body, and its thin lining and mucus act as a careful gate.

beats.scene: A small cartoon of tiny bacteria crowded together inside a long tube
beats.summary: Most gut microbes live in the large intestine, and the body holds about as many microbes as human cells.

beats.scene: Ines writes the word microbe and draws a circle around it
beats.summary: Microbes are living things too small to see; most are bacteria, and some are fungi and viruses.

beats.scene: Kofi measures a human hair beside a drawing of bacteria lined up across it
beats.summary: Dozens of bacteria could line up across the width of one human hair.

beats.scene: Ines holds up a jar of green soup with a label that reads Microbiome
beats.summary: The microbiome is the whole community of microbes in the gut, and each person's community is different.

beats.scene: Ines lists many different microbe names on a whiteboard in different colours
beats.summary: A single gut can hold hundreds of kinds of microbe, and each person's mix overlaps with others but is not identical.

beats.scene: A baby in a blanket is passed from a mother's arms to a father's
beats.summary: Babies pick up their first microbes at birth and from milk, touch and surroundings, and the community grows over the first years.

beats.scene: A toothbrush and a smiling mouth beside a drawing of tiny microbes on teeth
beats.summary: Microbes also live in the mouth, on skin and in other places, each place with its own community.

beats.scene: A dark cabinet with rubber gloves attached to its front panel
beats.summary: Many gut microbes cannot survive in air, so they are studied in sealed cabinets without oxygen.

beats.scene: Ines points to a long strand of coloured letters on a computer screen
beats.summary: Scientists can now identify gut microbes by reading their DNA, because many were never grown in a laboratory.

beats.scene: Noah writes I am never eating alone in his notebook on a tram
beats.summary: Noah realises that he shares every meal with a crowd, and writes it down as he rides home.

beats.scene: A friendly microbe waves while a spiky germ is pushed away by a crowd
beats.summary: Most microbes are harmless or helpful, and a crowd of good ones helps to keep harmful germs away.

beats.scene: Ines draws a crowded bus with a small spiky germ left standing outside
beats.summary: Gut microbes compete with newcomers for food and space, which helps to protect against harmful germs.

beats.scene: Noah washes his hands at a kitchen sink beside a chicken on a board
beats.summary: Harmful germs do exist, so washing hands, cooking meat through and keeping food cold prevent food poisoning.

beats.scene: A pot of beans beside a drawing of microbes holding forks
beats.summary: Gut microbes help to digest food that the body's own juices cannot break down.

beats.scene: Ines draws a pill bottle labelled K and B beside a gut
beats.summary: Some gut microbes make a few vitamins, such as vitamin K and some B vitamins, though most vitamins come from food.

beats.scene: A drawing of a gut surrounded by a ring of small shield-shaped immune cells
beats.summary: Much of the immune system sits near the gut, and microbes help to train it to tell friend from foe.

beats.scene: Kofi shows a chart where the number of microbes rises along the gut
beats.summary: Few microbes live in the stomach, more in the small intestine, and the most in the large intestine.

beats.scene: A balance scale with a green leaf on one side
beats.summary: Scientists have no single picture of a perfect microbiome, and the word healthy covers many different mixes.

beats.scene: Tomasz squirts hand gel on his bicycle handlebars outside a cafe
beats.summary: Clean does not mean sterile; washing is useful, but there is no need to fight every microbe in daily life.

beats.scene: Noah sketches a garden growing inside a drawing of a gut
beats.summary: Ines suggests thinking of the gut as a garden to tend, not a battlefield to fight, with three jobs for microbes.

beats.scene: Noah holds his stomach outside an office door, parcel in hand
beats.summary: Noah gets butterflies before an important delivery, which shows how feelings and the gut are connected.

beats.scene: Glowing dots join a head and a gut like a long telephone cable
beats.summary: The gut and brain talk through nerves, hormones and immune signals, and early research suggests food may affect mood, though much is unknown.

beats.scene: Ines traces a long line from a brain down to a gut
beats.summary: A long nerve called the vagus connects the brain to the gut, and many messages travel upward from the gut.

beats.scene: A gut wrapped in a net of tiny glowing nerve cells
beats.summary: The gut has its own network of hundreds of millions of nerve cells, sometimes called the second brain.

beats.scene: A clock beside a half-eaten plate and a glowing signal travelling up a wire
beats.summary: Hormones from the gut tell the brain when the stomach is full, but the message takes time, so eating slowly helps.

beats.scene: Mice in a clean cage beside a laboratory tray and a tiny bowl
beats.summary: Experiments on mice raised without microbes show that gut microbes can affect behaviour, but mice are not people.

beats.scene: A jar of yoghurt beside a notepad with a question mark
beats.summary: Small studies of probiotics and mood give mixed results, and nobody should treat low mood with yoghurt alone.

beats.scene: A student at an exam desk holds a worried stomach
beats.summary: Stress can upset the gut, causing cramps or loose stools, and gut pain is real even when stress is involved.

beats.scene: Noah writes a column of hungry, happy and tired faces in his notebook
beats.summary: Noah keeps a simple diary of meals and moods for a week, though Ines warns that a diary shows patterns, not proof.

beats.scene: Ines taps a sticker on a laptop that reads claims are not proof
beats.summary: Many internet claims about the gut and mood run far ahead of the science, so Ines advises regular meals, variety and patience.

beats.scene: A bowl of beans and oats with tiny cartoon microbes eating from it
beats.summary: Microbes feed on the parts of food that we cannot digest, mostly fibre.

beats.scene: A wheat stalk, a carrot and an apple lie beside a ruler
beats.summary: Fibre is the part of plant foods that we cannot digest; it comes in different kinds, such as the soluble and insoluble kinds.

beats.scene: Ines lays out jars of leaves, oats and apple slices with different coloured labels
beats.summary: Fibre is not one thing but many, such as cellulose in leaves, pectin in apples and beta-glucan in oats.

beats.scene: Ines stirs oats in a glass of water beside wheat bran
beats.summary: Soluble fibre dissolves in water and forms a gel, while insoluble fibre adds bulk and stays rough.

beats.scene: Noah looks at a cheese sandwich with slices of ham on white bread
beats.summary: Animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy contain no fibre at all, so the fibre in a diet comes only from plants.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines push a trolley past shelves of bread
beats.summary: In a supermarket Ines shows that white bread has lost much of its fibre, while wholemeal bread keeps more.

beats.scene: Noah reads the back of a bread packet
beats.summary: On a label, the first ingredient is the biggest, and about six grams of fibre per hundred grams counts as high.

beats.scene: A heart and a fork drawn beside a bowl of oats
beats.summary: Fibre does more than feed microbes: it helps people feel full, may steady blood sugar and, in oats, may lower cholesterol.

beats.scene: A jar of fibre powder beside a bowl of mixed beans and a spoon
beats.summary: A fibre powder is not the same as whole plant foods, which bring many fibres and other nutrients together.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines carry oats and lentils out of the shop
beats.summary: Noah buys his first high-fibre foods, oats and dried lentils, and wonders how microbes eat.

beats.scene: A bowl of bread dough rising with bubbles beside a warm oven
beats.summary: Microbes break down fibre by fermentation, a process that works without oxygen and that also makes bread rise.

beats.scene: Ines writes the words short-chain fatty acids on a whiteboard in green
beats.summary: Fermenting fibre makes short-chain fatty acids, which feed the cells lining the large intestine and may help to calm inflammation.

beats.scene: A single cell on a plate eating a glowing yellow drop labelled butyrate
beats.summary: Butyrate, one of these acids, is a favourite fuel for the cells of the colon.

beats.scene: A bloodstream drawn as a river carrying small glowing drops to a heart
beats.summary: Some short-chain fatty acids reach the blood and may affect appetite and blood sugar, though much of this evidence is early.

beats.scene: A cartoon bubble of air rises from a pot of beans on a stove
beats.summary: Wind is a normal result of microbes fermenting fibre, and most people pass wind many times a day.

beats.scene: A paper plate with eggs and cabbage beside a puzzled nose
beats.summary: Most gut gas has no smell; the odour comes from small amounts of sulphur compounds, and a smell alone is not a sign of illness.

beats.scene: A balloon stretched over a bottle of sugar water
beats.summary: Kofi shows how fermentation makes gas that can inflate a balloon.

beats.scene: A chain of tiny microbes passing a glowing parcel along
beats.summary: Microbes pass food along in chains, because the waste of one kind becomes the meal of another.

beats.scene: Ines lines up jars of different fibres, each with its own microbe
beats.summary: Different fibres feed different microbes, which is why a mixed diet supports a mixed community.

beats.scene: Noah writes a thank-you note in his notebook beside a plate of lentils
beats.summary: Noah writes a thank-you note to his microbes and resolves to feed them more fibre, but Ines warns that the amount matters.

beats.scene: A measuring bar shows thirty grams next to a small bowl of cereal
beats.summary: Many national guides advise about thirty grams of fibre a day for adults, and most adults eat less.

beats.scene: A table set with porridge, a wholemeal sandwich, a bean stew and an apple
beats.summary: A day of porridge, wholemeal bread, a bean stew, an apple and nuts can come close to thirty grams.

beats.scene: Noah writes numbers in a notebook beside a crisp packet and a sandwich
beats.summary: Noah checks the fibre in his usual week and finds that he eats far less than the guides suggest.

beats.scene: A shelf of white bread, biscuits and ready meals
beats.summary: Many everyday foods, especially refined and highly processed ones, are low in fibre, which helps to explain why many people eat less than the guides.

beats.scene: A table of fibre guides from different countries
beats.summary: Guides in different countries give slightly different targets, and children need less than adults.

beats.scene: A doctor's door with a small sign reading ask first
beats.summary: Some people are told to eat less fibre for a time, for example after bowel operations, and should follow their doctor.

beats.scene: Noah holds a bag of popcorn beside a bag of crisps
beats.summary: Easy swaps add fibre: wholemeal for white bread, brown for white rice, popcorn for crisps.

beats.scene: Tomasz peers into Noah's popcorn bag on a kerb
beats.summary: Tomasz teases Noah about his popcorn, then asks for a handful.

beats.scene: Ines points to a label reading added fibre on a bar
beats.summary: Fibre can be added to foods, but whole foods bring other nutrients and are usually the better choice.

beats.scene: A paper on a fridge door with a small ladder drawn on it
beats.summary: Noah plans to add a little fibre every few days and posts the plan on his fridge.

beats.scene: Noah adds beans to a plate beside a tall glass of water
beats.summary: Fibre should be increased slowly over weeks, with plenty of water, so the gut can adjust.

beats.scene: Noah stirs an enormous pot of chilli with a wooden spoon
beats.summary: Noah is too eager and eats a huge bean chilli on his first evening, and pays for it with a bloated, noisy night.

beats.scene: Ines holds a tiny spoonful of beans beside a large plate
beats.summary: Microbes and gut muscles need time to adjust, so small steps work better than big ones.

beats.scene: A tin of beans being rinsed under a tap in a colander
beats.summary: Beans and lentils are rich in fibre, and starting with small portions, and rinsing tinned beans, helps the gut to adapt.

beats.scene: A pot of red kidney beans boiling hard with a timer beside it
beats.summary: Dried beans need soaking and boiling, and raw or undercooked red kidney beans are poisonous and must be boiled hard.

beats.scene: A pan of red lentils turning into a golden soup with carrots and onion
beats.summary: Lentils need no soaking and cook quickly, so Noah makes a simple lentil soup.

beats.scene: Noah ticks a small chart on the wall with numbers for wind each day
beats.summary: Noah keeps a simple record of wind, and finds that it is worse in the first week and then settles as his gut adapts.

beats.scene: Pavel holds a tub of lentil soup in the courier office kitchen
beats.summary: Pavel and the other couriers hear about Noah's soup, and several of them ask for the recipe.

beats.scene: A person on a sofa holds their stomach, looking worried
beats.summary: If bloating or pain does not settle, or is severe, step back, and see a doctor if it does not improve.

beats.scene: Noah looks at a notebook page with a rising line and a smiling face
beats.summary: After two weeks Noah is eating more fibre, drinking more water, and feels the first small differences.

beats.scene: A wooden bowl of oats beside brown rice and pearl barley in jars
beats.summary: Whole grains such as oats, barley and brown rice keep their fibre, and oats and barley contain a fibre called beta-glucan.

beats.scene: A drawing of a grain split into three coloured layers
beats.summary: A whole grain has a fibre-rich outer layer, a germ and a starchy centre, and refining removes the first two.

beats.scene: Noah stirs a pot of porridge with a spoon and a worried look
beats.summary: Noah makes his first pot of porridge, with oats and water, and learns to add fruit rather than a spoon of sugar.

beats.scene: A row of jars labelled rye, buckwheat, quinoa and barley
beats.summary: Other grains and seeds, such as rye, buckwheat, quinoa and barley, add variety, and pearl barley is cheap and good in soups.

beats.scene: Noah bites into a crunchy apple with the skin on beside carrots
beats.summary: Fruit and vegetables bring fibre, and eating the skins where safe adds more; different ones feed different microbes.

beats.scene: A freezer drawer packed with frozen peas, spinach and mixed vegetables
beats.summary: Frozen vegetables keep their fibre and are cheap, convenient and just as good as fresh, so they suit a busy courier.

beats.scene: A plate of hummus, carrot sticks and a small bowl of chickpeas
beats.summary: Chickpeas and other pulses are cheap and rich in fibre, and hummus with vegetable sticks makes an easy snack.

beats.scene: A small pile of seeds and nuts beside a jar of chia and flax
beats.summary: Nuts and seeds add fibre and healthy fats; ground or soaked seeds are easier to digest, and nut allergies are serious.

beats.scene: Ines compares a whole orange with a glass of orange juice on the counter
beats.summary: The closer a food is to its original plant form, the more fibre it keeps; whole fruit is better than juice.

beats.scene: Noah checks his weekly fibre total beside a fridge that is full of plants
beats.summary: After a few weeks of changes, Noah's fibre has climbed to about twenty grams a day, and Ines says that variety comes next.

beats.scene: Ines hands Noah a paper with a list of plant names in colours
beats.summary: Variety matters because different microbes like different fibres, and a varied diet feeds a more varied community.

beats.scene: A bar chart on a screen compares two groups of people
beats.summary: A large survey found that people eating more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied gut community, though this is a link, not proof.

beats.scene: Ines draws an ice cream beside a sunburned nose on the whiteboard
beats.summary: A link is not proof: people who eat many plants may differ in other ways, so the survey cannot show that plants alone cause the difference.

beats.scene: Noah and Ines read a list of plants labelled count and do not count
beats.summary: Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, beans, grains, fruit and vegetables all count as different plants, and thirty is a marker and not a magic number.

beats.scene: Noah sticks a chart to his fridge and ticks the names of plants
beats.summary: Noah starts a weekly plant count; herbs, spices, nuts and seeds all count as different plants.

beats.scene: A shopper holds up bags of mixed beans and mixed seeds
beats.summary: Mixed bags of beans, seeds, frozen vegetables and salad leaves are an easy way to add many plants at once.

beats.scene: Noah looks at a strange knobbly vegetable on a market stall
beats.summary: At the street market Noah buys a vegetable that he cannot name, and the stallholder tells him how to cook it.

beats.scene: A rack of spice jars beside a pan
beats.summary: Herbs and spices count towards the total, and they make plant food tasty.

beats.scene: Tomasz and Pavel point to a whiteboard with names and plant scores
beats.summary: Tomasz challenges Noah to a plant-count contest, and the couriers' office joins in with a scoreboard.

beats.scene: Noah ticks the last box on a nearly full chart beside a smiling Ines
beats.summary: Ines warns that thirty is a marker and not a test, that people with certain conditions may need advice, and Noah reaches twenty-two plants.

beats.scene: A tropical rainforest and a bare field of one crop shown side by side
beats.summary: A varied microbiome is generally linked with better health, much like a rainforest is more resilient than a single-crop field.

beats.scene: A thermometer with a green zone beside a drawing of a gut
beats.summary: Diversity is a useful clue but not a score to chase, because a high number does not always mean better health.

beats.scene: A small stormy cloud over a field and a rainforest with a rainbow
beats.summary: A diverse gut community seems better at recovering after a disturbance such as illness or antibiotics, though the evidence is still growing.

beats.scene: Ines holds a photograph of a camp beside a map of Tanzania
beats.summary: Studies of traditional communities such as the Hadza in Tanzania found more varied gut microbes, though their lives differ in many ways.

beats.scene: Garlic, leeks, onions and asparagus laid out beside a green banana on a board
beats.summary: Prebiotics are fibres that feed helpful microbes; onions, garlic, leeks, oats and slightly green bananas contain them.

beats.scene: A cut onion beside a bulb of garlic and a chicory root with arrows
beats.summary: Prebiotic fibres such as inulin are found in onions, garlic, leeks, chicory and Jerusalem artichokes, which can cause a lot of wind.

beats.scene: Kofi shows a plate with a bright pink group of microbes labelled Bifidobacteria
beats.summary: Kofi explains that Bifidobacteria are one group of microbes that thrive on fibres such as inulin, and are common in the guts of babies.

beats.scene: A drawing of a jar of prebiotic powder
beats.summary: Prebiotic supplements are heavily advertised, but whole foods come first, and the evidence for powders is mixed.

beats.scene: A bowl of onion soup beside a printed card reading some people react
beats.summary: Some people with irritable bowel syndrome react to prebiotic foods such as onions and garlic, and should get advice from a doctor or dietitian.

beats.scene: Noah's sister Mara and her small son stand in his doorway
beats.summary: Noah's sister Mara visits with her son Leo, and cannot believe the smell of garlic, leeks and soup in his flat.

beats.scene: A cooled bowl of boiled potatoes, rice and pasta in a fridge
beats.summary: Resistant starch survives digestion and feeds microbes; cooked and cooled potatoes, rice and pasta, and slightly green bananas contain more of it.

beats.scene: Two pots of steaming potatoes beside a small thermometer and a clock
beats.summary: As starch cools it changes its structure, and reheating keeps at least some of the resistant starch.

beats.scene: A tray of cooked rice cooling by an open window beside a fridge
beats.summary: Cooked rice must be cooled quickly, kept in the fridge and eaten within a day, because bacteria that survive cooking can make a person ill.

beats.scene: Mara and Leo eat potato salad at a kitchen table while Noah serves
beats.summary: Noah makes a potato salad with the skins on for Sunday lunch, and Mara and her son enjoy it.

beats.scene: Purple cabbage, blueberries, green tea and dark chocolate in a row
beats.summary: Polyphenols are colourful plant substances; gut microbes change them into other substances, and research on their effects is promising but young.

beats.scene: Lemon juice turns a glass of purple cabbage juice pink
beats.summary: A purple cabbage juice changes colour with acid and alkali, a way of seeing a plant pigment at work.

beats.scene: A rainbow of vegetables laid out on a kitchen counter
beats.summary: Choosing foods of many colours is a simple way to get a variety of plants, though colour alone does not guarantee anything.

beats.scene: A cup of tea and a cup of coffee beside olives
beats.summary: Tea, coffee, olive oil, cocoa, nuts and berries also contain polyphenols, and moderate amounts are fine for most adults.

beats.scene: A glass of red wine with a cross drawn beside it
beats.summary: Alcohol is not a health food, so the polyphenols in red wine are not a reason to drink it.

beats.scene: Noah checks a plate of colourful food beside a chart showing twenty-five plants
beats.summary: Noah's plate now looks like a painter's palette, his plant count has reached twenty-five, and Tomasz says that he looks like a salad.

beats.scene: Kimchi, sauerkraut, kefir and yoghurt jars on a shelf in a market stall
beats.summary: Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso contain live microbes, and some of them may help the gut.

beats.scene: Dara smiles behind a market stall holding a jar of red kimchi
beats.summary: The stallholder Dara explains how she makes kimchi and sauerkraut at home from cabbage, salt and time.

beats.scene: Noah reads the label on a jar and Dara points to the word live
beats.summary: Not every fermented food contains live microbes: bread is baked, and many pickles are made with vinegar or are heat-treated, so labels should be read.

beats.scene: A jar of bubbling cabbage on a counter with a cloth over the top
beats.summary: Kimchi is made from cabbage, salt, garlic, ginger and chilli, and bubbles as it ferments in a jar for days.

beats.scene: A glass of kefir beside a bowl of yoghurt and a spoon
beats.summary: Kefir is a tangy drink made from milk and small grains of microbes, and it often contains more kinds of microbe than ordinary yoghurt.

beats.scene: Ines points to a chart of rising bars on a laboratory wall

beats.scene: A bowl of miso soup with tofu and green onions steaming on a counter

beats.scene: Ines and Noah read a shelf of pill bottles labelled probiotic in a pharmacy

beats.scene: Ines points at a long Latin name and a code on a bottle

beats.scene: A calm patient with a glass of water and a small bottle
beats.summary: Some probiotic strains have been shown in trials to help with problems such as diarrhoea after antibiotics, but results differ from product to product.

beats.scene: A magnifier held over a pharmacy label

beats.scene: Noah packs shredded cabbage into a clean glass jar with salt

beats.scene: A jar of cabbage with small bubbles, leaves held under brine
beats.summary: Fermenting cabbage must stay under its brine, and bubbles and a sour smell are normal.

beats.scene: Noah smells an open jar while Ines and Kofi watch

beats.scene: A doctor hands a small box of tablets labelled antibiotics to Mara

beats.scene: Ines holds a small box of tablets beside a hospital corridor drawing
beats.summary: Antibiotics save lives but also disturb gut microbes; take them only when a doctor prescribes them and follow the instructions.

beats.scene: A calendar with a few boxes ticked and a gentle arrow pointing forward

beats.scene: Ines stands in a supermarket aisle full of brightly coloured packets

beats.scene: A slice of cake and a fizzy drink beside a bowl of lentils

beats.summary: No food is a villain: enjoying a treat is fine, and swaps that add plants matter more than rules that cause worry.

beats.scene: Noah sleeps in bed while cartoon microbes float calmly above his head

beats.summary: Warning signs can have many causes, most of them treatable, and checking early is better than waiting; they are not a reason to panic.

beats.scene: A baby sleeps in a cot while a parent holds a bottle
beats.summary: A baby's microbes begin to form at birth, and a baby's diet should follow advice from a doctor or health visitor.

beats.summary: Eating out can still be gut-friendly: choose beans, vegetables, whole grains and a side salad when you can.

beats.summary: Gut-friendly food can be cheap: dried beans, oats, frozen vegetables, cabbage and carrots.

B1B2: Noah rides a bicycle through the city all day, and he usually eats a quick sandwich at a red light. Lately he has started to wonder what all this fast food is doing inside his body.
Pavel, the dispatcher, sends Noah a new delivery every few minutes from the office. There is never a good moment to sit down, so lunch is whatever fits in one hand.
Noah's stomach rumbles so loudly outside the post office that his friend Tomasz stops talking. Tomasz is another courier, and he laughs and says that it sounds like a small motorbike.
That evening Noah carries his bicycle up the stairs and meets his neighbour Ines on the landing. She is holding a heavy shopping bag filled with beans, onions and green leaves.
Noah asks Ines a question that has been bothering him all week, which is what happens to a sandwich after he swallows it. Ines smiles and says that he is not asking about a body but about a crowd.

Ines makes Noah an offer on the landing, which is six weeks of lessons in return for small changes to his meals. She promises to be honest about one thing in particular, which is saying when science does not know the answer.
On Saturday morning Noah locks his bicycle outside the university and follows Ines along a long corridor. The air smells of soap, and every glass door has a small sign with a long, difficult name.
Ines's student Kofi puts a drop of plain yoghurt under a microscope and lets Noah look. He sees thousands of tiny shapes, and he is amazed to learn that they are alive.
Ines gives Noah a green notebook and three rules for the next six weeks. He must be curious, he must be careful, and he must be kind to his own gut.

Outside in the afternoon sun, Noah opens the notebook on a bench and writes the date at the top of the first page. Beneath it he writes a single question, which is what happens to my lunch after I swallow it.
On Sunday morning Ines draws a long, winding tube on the whiteboard in her kitchen. She explains that the gut runs from the mouth to the end of the body and is several metres long.
Ines gives Noah a plain cracker and asks him to chew it for a full minute. Slowly it begins to taste sweet, because saliva has started to break the starch into sugars.
After a swallow, food does not simply fall down the throat. Muscles in the gullet squeeze it along in waves, which is why people can swallow even when they are upside down.
The stomach is a stretchy bag that churns the food and mixes it with strong acid. The acid kills many of the microbes that arrive with a meal, and the food stays there for a few hours.
The small intestine is a long, narrow tube where most of the food is broken down and taken into the blood. Its walls are covered in tiny folds and fingers, which give it a huge surface.
Other organs help the small intestine to do its work. The liver makes a liquid called bile that helps with fats, and the pancreas sends juices that break down starch, fat and protein.
Not everything in a meal can be broken down by the body's own juices. The parts that cannot be digested, mostly fibre, travel on to the next part of the gut.
The large intestine is wider than the small intestine, and it frames it like a picture frame. It takes water back from the leftovers, and it is where most of the gut's microbes live.

Ines says that the whole journey often takes a day or two, although it varies from person to person. Sweetcorn is a good way to see the idea, because the tough yellow skins pass through without being digested.
Ines tells Noah that the inside of the gut is, in a sense, still outside the body. A thin lining with a layer of mucus acts as a careful gate that lets in useful things and keeps out the rest.
Ines draws a crowd of tiny dots inside the large intestine and says that this is where most gut microbes live. By recent estimates, the body holds about as many microbes as it does human cells.
A microbe is a living thing that is far too small to see without a microscope. Most gut microbes are bacteria, but there are also fungi and viruses in the mix.
Kofi shows Noah a single hair from his own head under the microscope. Dozens of bacteria could stand side by side across its width, which explains why nobody saw them for centuries.

Ines holds up a jar of green soup labelled Microbiome and explains that it means all the microbes living in and on a person. Like the soup, it has many ingredients, and no two people have exactly the same mix.

One person's gut can hold hundreds of different kinds of microbe, and they live together like the members of a large family. Two people share many of them, but each person's own mix is a little different.
A baby begins life with very few microbes, and picks up more at birth and from milk, touch and surroundings. The community grows and changes over the first few years of life.

Microbes are not only in the gut, because the mouth and the skin each have their own communities. Brushing teeth twice a day keeps the mouth community in balance, so Ines says that Noah should keep doing it.

Many microbes of the large intestine cannot survive in fresh air, because they have adapted to a place with almost no oxygen. Scientists keep them in sealed cabinets, so Kofi works with his hands inside rubber gloves.
Many gut microbes have never been grown in a laboratory, so scientists now read their DNA to find out who is there. Ines shows Noah a screen with long strings of coloured letters, each one a clue.
On the tram home, Noah opens his notebook and writes that he is never eating alone. He thinks about the crowd inside him, and for the first time he wonders what it wants for dinner.
Ines tells Noah that most microbes are harmless and many are helpful, and only a few cause disease. A large, healthy crowd can also crowd out harmful germs, so that they find it hard to settle.
Ines draws a bus that is already full of friendly passengers, with a spiky germ left outside. This is a simple picture of how the gut's own microbes compete with newcomers for food and for space.
Ines is quick to add that harmful germs do exist, and that they can cause food poisoning. Washing hands, cooking meat all the way through and keeping food cold are simple ways to avoid them.
The first job of gut microbes is to help with digestion. They break down some of the plant food that the body's own juices cannot manage, and in return they get a meal.
Some gut microbes make a few vitamins, such as vitamin K and several of the B vitamins. Most of the vitamins that a person needs still come from food, so microbes are a bonus and not a replacement.

A large part of the body's immune system sits close to the gut, where it meets food and microbes every day. Early in life, microbes seem to help it to learn which things are friends and which are not.

Kofi shows a chart of the gut in which the number of microbes rises from one end to the other. There are few in the acid of the stomach, more in the small intestine and by far the most in the large intestine.
Noah asks what a perfect microbiome looks like, and Ines says that nobody knows. Healthy people have many different mixes, so scientists look for patterns instead of a single ideal.
Tomasz is so afraid of germs that he cleans his handlebars with hand gel every hour. Ines says that sensible washing is good, but there is no need to fight every microbe in everyday life.
Ines tells Noah that it is better to think of the gut as a garden to tend than as a battlefield. Its microbes do three jobs, which are digesting, making a few vitamins and training the immune system.
Before an important delivery to a large office, Noah feels butterflies in his stomach. He has noticed this before, and he asks Ines why a feeling in the head can be felt in the belly.
The gut and the brain send messages to each other through nerves, hormones and the immune system. Early research asks whether gut microbes affect mood, but much is still unknown.
Ines draws a long nerve that runs from the brain down through the neck to the gut. It is called the vagus nerve, and many of the messages on it travel upward, from the gut to the brain.

The wall of the gut contains its own network of nerve cells, hundreds of millions of them. It is sometimes called a second brain, although it does not think or have feelings in the way that the brain does.

As food moves through the gut, cells in its lining send hormones to the brain to say that the body is getting full. The message takes a little time to arrive, so people who eat very fast can easily eat too much.

Kofi explains that scientists have raised mice with no gut microbes at all, and that these mice behave differently from normal mice. This shows that microbes can affect the brain, but mice are not people.

Some small studies have tested probiotics for mood and anxiety, and the results so far are mixed. Ines says that nobody should treat low mood with yoghurt alone, and anyone who feels low for long should talk to a doctor.

Stress can upset the gut, so that some people get cramps or loose stools before an exam or a big event. The pain is real, even when stress is part of the cause, and nobody should be told that it is only imaginary.
Ines suggests that Noah keep a simple diary for a week, noting what he eats and how he feels. She warns that a diary can show patterns, but that it cannot prove that one thing causes another.
Ines warns Noah that many claims online about the gut and the brain run far ahead of the science. Her advice is modest, which is to eat regular meals, enjoy a variety of foods and be patient.
The microbes of the large intestine have to eat too, and they feed on what the body leaves behind. Most of that leftover food is fibre, which comes only from plants.
Fibre is the part of plant foods that human digestion cannot break down, and it comes in several different kinds. Ines lays out a stalk of wheat, a carrot and an apple to show where some of it hides.
Fibre is not a single substance but a large family. Leaves contain cellulose, apples contain pectin and oats contain beta-glucan, and different microbes prefer different kinds.
Soluble fibre mixes with water and forms a soft gel, as when oats thicken in a pan. Insoluble fibre does not dissolve, and it adds bulk that helps food to move along.
Ines points out that meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods contain no fibre at all. Fibre comes only from plants, so a meal of ham and cheese on white bread offers the microbes very little.

On Saturday, Ines takes Noah to a supermarket and stops in front of the shelves of bread. White flour has had much of the outer part of the grain removed, so wholemeal and wholegrain breads keep more fibre.

Ines shows Noah how to read a label, beginning with the list of ingredients, where the first item is the largest. In many countries, a food with about six grams of fibre per hundred grams can be called high in fibre.
Fibre does more than feed microbes, because it also helps people to feel full for longer. Soluble fibre, such as the beta-glucan in oats, may help to steady blood sugar and to lower cholesterol.

Noah wonders whether he could simply buy a tub of fibre powder and stir it into his coffee. Ines says that whole foods bring many kinds of fibre together with vitamins and minerals, which a single powder cannot match.
Noah buys a bag of oats and a bag of dried lentils, his first purchases for his new project. On the way home, he asks how microbes can possibly eat, because they have no mouths and no forks.
Ines explains that microbes eat fibre by fermenting it, which means breaking it down without oxygen. It is the same kind of process that makes bread dough rise and turns milk into yoghurt.
When microbes ferment fibre, they make substances called short-chain fatty acids. These feed the cells that line the large intestine, and they may also help to calm inflammation in the body.
One of these acids is called butyrate, and the cells that line the colon use it as a favourite fuel. Ines says that these cells get a large share of their energy from what the microbes make.

A small amount of these acids passes into the blood and travels around the body. They may affect appetite and blood sugar, although much of the evidence comes from laboratory studies and is still early.
When microbes ferment fibre, they also make gases, so a little wind is entirely normal. Most healthy people pass wind many times a day, and nothing is wrong with them.
Most gut gas is hydrogen and carbon dioxide, which have no smell at all. The smell comes from tiny amounts of sulphur gases made from eggs, meat or cabbage, and it is not a sign of illness.
Kofi mixes warm water, sugar and a spoonful of yeast in a bottle and fixes a balloon over the top. After half an hour the balloon begins to swell, because the yeast ferments the sugar and makes gas.
Ines describes how gut microbes work in teams, because the waste made by one kind can become a meal for another. Together they form a long chain that breaks down fibre step by step.
Not every microbe can eat every kind of fibre, so each kind of fibre feeds its own group. A diet with many fibres therefore supports a larger and more varied community.

That night Noah writes a short thank-you note to his microbes and decides to feed them more fibre. Ines, who reads it over his shoulder, warns him that the amount matters, and that more is not always better.
Ines tells Noah that many national guides advise adults to eat about thirty grams of fibre a day. Most adults eat less than that, and in many countries the average is far below it.
Ines writes out a day of meals that could come close to thirty grams. It includes porridge, a wholemeal sandwich, a bean stew, an apple with its skin and a handful of nuts.
Noah spends three days writing down everything that he eats and looking up its fibre on the packets. His usual average comes to about eleven grams a day, which is far below the guides.

Ines explains why most people fall short of the target, and the reasons are quite ordinary. Many everyday foods, such as white bread, biscuits and ready meals, have lost their fibre or never had much, and busy people reach for them.

Ines shows Noah that guides in different countries suggest slightly different amounts, often between about twenty-five and thirty-eight grams. Children need less than adults, so parents should check the advice for their child's age.
Ines adds an important warning to the thirty-gram target. A few people are told to eat less fibre for a time, for example after a bowel operation, and they should follow their doctor.

Ines suggests swaps, because it is easier to change what one eats than to add a whole new meal. Wholemeal bread can replace white bread, brown rice can replace white rice, and plain popcorn, which is a whole grain, can replace crisps.
Tomasz finds Noah on the kerb with a bag of popcorn and teases him about the change. Within a minute he is asking for a handful, and he admits that it is better than crisps.
Some foods, such as bars and drinks, have fibre added to them, often in the form of a powder made from plant roots. Ines says that these are not bad, but whole foods bring more with the fibre.
Noah writes a plan on a sheet of paper and sticks it to his fridge. It says that he will add a little more fibre every few days, and drink water, and see how he feels.
On Monday, Ines reminds Noah that fibre should be added slowly, over a few weeks, with plenty of water. A gut that is used to very little needs time to adjust.
Noah ignores the advice and cooks an enormous bean chilli on the first evening. He eats two large bowls, and by midnight his stomach is tight and very noisy.
Ines explains that the microbes in his gut need time to grow into the new menu, and the gut muscles need time to adjust too. A sudden change gives them no time at all, so small steps work better.

Beans and lentils are rich in fibre, and Ines tells Noah to start with just a few spoonfuls. She also suggests rinsing tinned beans in a colander, which washes away some of the substances that cause gas.

Ines warns Noah that dried beans need to be soaked overnight, drained and boiled properly. Raw or undercooked red kidney beans contain a natural poison, so they must be boiled hard for at least ten minutes.
Lentils need no soaking and cook in about twenty minutes, so they suit a busy cyclist. Noah makes a simple soup of red lentils, carrots and onions, and it turns golden in the pan.
Noah makes a small chart to record how much wind he has each day. It is worse in the first week, and by the second week it has begun to settle as his gut adapts.
At the courier office, Noah shares a tub of lentil soup with Pavel and Tomasz. Pavel asks for the recipe, and soon half the office is talking about beans and lentils.
Ines tells Noah that a little wind and fullness are normal while the gut adjusts. If there is pain, or the discomfort does not settle after a few weeks, he should eat less fibre and see a doctor.
After two weeks, Noah is eating more fibre and drinking more water, and his stomach is calmer. He has not turned into a new person, but he notices that his afternoons are slightly less heavy.
Whole grains such as oats, barley and brown rice keep the outer layers where most of the fibre is found. Oats and barley also contain beta-glucan, the fibre that forms a soft gel.
A whole grain has three parts, which are the bran, the germ and the starchy centre. Refining removes the bran and the germ, which is why white flour has so much less fibre.
Noah makes his first pot of porridge, and it comes out so thick that the spoon stands up in it. By adding more water and a sliced banana, he finds a version that he actually enjoys.
Ines shows Noah other grains and seeds such as rye, buckwheat, quinoa and barley. Pearl barley is cheap, keeps for a long time, and is excellent in soups and stews.
Fruit and vegetables bring fibre too, and the skins of many of them contain extra. If the skins are washed well, Noah can eat apples, pears and carrots without peeling them.
Ines tells Noah that frozen vegetables keep their fibre and are usually frozen soon after they are picked. They are cheap and quick to cook, so they suit a courier who has no time to chop.
Chickpeas belong to the same family of pulses as beans and lentils, and they are rich in fibre. Hummus made from chickpeas, with carrot sticks to dip, becomes an easy snack for Noah's bicycle bag.
Nuts and seeds add fibre and healthy fats, and Noah sprinkles a spoonful over his porridge. Ground or soaked seeds are easier to digest, and nuts can be dangerous to anyone with an allergy.
Ines shows Noah the simple rule that the closer a food is to the plant that it came from, the more fibre it keeps. A whole orange has much more fibre than a glass of orange juice.
By the end of the week Noah's fibre has risen to about twenty grams a day. Ines is pleased, and says that the next step is not more fibre but more variety.

Ines hands Noah a long list of plants, each one written in its own colour. She explains that variety matters, because different microbes like different fibres and a varied diet feeds a more varied community.

Ines shows Noah the results of a large citizen-science survey in which thousands of people recorded their diets. Those who ate more than thirty kinds of plant a week had a more varied gut community than those who ate ten or fewer.
Ines explains that a link is not the same as proof, and she draws an ice cream beside a sunburned nose. Ice cream sales and sunburn rise together, but the sun causes both.

Ines explains that every kind of plant counts, including fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds, beans, grains, herbs and spices. The figure of thirty is a marker from one survey, and it is not a magic number.
Noah starts a chart on his fridge to count the different plants that he eats in a week. Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, beans and grains all count, so the numbers grow faster than he expected.
Noah discovers that mixed bags are an easy way to raise his score. A tin of mixed beans, a bag of mixed seeds and a pack of mixed salad leaves each bring several plants at once.
On Saturday Noah visits the street market and buys a knobbly vegetable that he cannot name. The woman at the stall tells him how to cook it, and he adds a new plant to his chart.
Herbs and spices count as plants, and Noah starts to use cumin, paprika, parsley and mint. A pinch adds very little fibre, but it makes vegetables and beans taste so good that he eats more of them.

Tomasz hears about the chart and challenges Noah to a contest to see who can eat the most kinds of plant in a week. Pavel draws a scoreboard on the office whiteboard, and soon five couriers are competing.

Noah ends the week with twenty-two plants and wins the contest by one point. Ines congratulates him, but reminds him that thirty is a marker and not a test, and that some people with bowel conditions need personal advice.

Ines draws a rainforest full of different trees, animals and insects beside a field with only one crop. A varied gut community is a bit like the rainforest, because it is generally linked with better health.
Ines warns Noah that diversity is a useful clue, but it is not a score to chase. A very high number does not always mean better health, and nobody can say what the ideal number is.

Ines says that a varied community seems to recover better after a disturbance, such as an illness or a course of antibiotics. Researchers are still collecting evidence, but the idea fits what is known from nature.

Ines tells Noah about studies of traditional communities such as the Hadza in Tanzania, who eat many wild plants. Their gut microbes were more varied than those of many city dwellers, though their lives differ in countless other ways.
Prebiotics are fibres that feed helpful microbes, and Ines lays out garlic, leeks, onions and asparagus on the board. A slightly green banana, which is not yet sweet, is another good example.

One well-known prebiotic fibre is called inulin, and it is found in onions, garlic, leeks and chicory. Jerusalem artichokes are rich in it too, though they are famous for causing a great deal of wind.
Kofi shows Noah a group of microbes called Bifidobacteria, which grow well on fibres such as inulin. They are common in the guts of babies, and many scientists see them as friendly microbes.
Noah sees an advertisement for a prebiotic powder that promises a perfect gut in two weeks. Ines says that whole foods come first, and that the evidence for such powders is mixed.

Ines adds a warning that some people with irritable bowel syndrome react badly to foods such as onions, garlic and beans. If that is the case, they should ask a doctor or dietitian for a plan, because cutting out foods without help can do harm.
Noah's older sister Mara visits with her small son Leo on Sunday, and she stops in the doorway. The kitchen smells of garlic and leeks, and she asks what has happened to her brother.

Ines introduces resistant starch, a kind of starch that is not digested in the small intestine and travels on to feed the microbes. Cooked and cooled potatoes, rice and pasta contain more of it, and so do slightly green bananas.

When cooked starch cools down, its structure changes into a form that is harder to digest. Reheating the food keeps at least some of this resistant starch, so a hot meal made from cooled leftovers still counts.
Ines gives Noah a safety rule about cooked rice. It must be cooled within an hour and eaten within a day, because bacteria that survive cooking can make people ill.
For Sunday lunch Noah makes a potato salad with the skins left on, cooled in the fridge and mixed with herbs, yoghurt and spring onions. Mara is surprised by how good it is, and Leo asks for more.

Polyphenols are colourful substances in plants such as purple cabbage, blueberries, green tea and dark chocolate. Gut microbes change them into other substances, and research on their effects is promising but young.

Kofi boils purple cabbage and pours the juice into three glasses. A little lemon juice turns one pink, and a pinch of baking soda turns another blue-green, which shows that plant colours are real chemicals.

Ines gives Noah a simple rule, which is to put as many colours as possible on the plate. It is only a rough guide, because a food's colour does not guarantee what is inside it, but it helps him to vary his meals.

Tea, coffee, olive oil, cocoa, nuts and berries all contain polyphenols. Ines says that moderate amounts are fine for most adults, although anyone who is pregnant or on medicine should ask a doctor about caffeine.
Noah asks about red wine, which is often said to contain helpful polyphenols. Ines says that alcohol is not a health food, and that grapes, berries and tea are a much safer way to get them.

By the end of the week, Noah's plate looks like a painter's palette and his plant count has reached twenty-five. Tomasz says that he is starting to look like a salad, but he secretly asks for the potato recipe.

On Saturday Ines takes Noah to a stall at the street market that is crowded with jars. Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso contain live microbes, and some of them may help the gut.
The stallholder is called Dara, and she makes her own kimchi and sauerkraut from cabbage, salt and a little patience. She tells Noah that the microbes already on the cabbage do most of the work.

Dara explains that not every fermented food still contains live microbes. Bread is baked, and many shop pickles are made with vinegar or are heat-treated, so it helps to look for the words live or unpasteurised.
Dara shows Noah a photograph of her kitchen, where jars of kimchi sit on the counter. It is made from cabbage, salt, garlic, ginger and chilli, and it bubbles gently for several days as it ferments.
Kefir is a tangy drink made by adding small grains of microbes to milk. It usually contains a wider mix of microbes than ordinary yoghurt, and there are also versions made from soya milk or water.
Back at the laboratory, Ines points to a chart of rising bars. In a small university trial, people who ate more fermented foods for ten weeks had a greater variety of gut microbes at the end.
Ines is careful to point out that the trial was small and short, with only a few dozen adults. Results need to be repeated, and what helps one person may not help another.

Ines reminds Noah that fermented vegetables, such as sauerkraut and kimchi, can be high in salt. People who have been told to limit salt, for example because of high blood pressure, should check the label and ask their doctor.
Dara sells Noah a tub of miso, a fermented paste made from soya beans. At home he stirs it into a soup with tofu after the heat is off, because boiling can kill the live microbes.

Noah starts small, with a spoonful of kimchi, some live yoghurt or a small glass of kefir each day. Ines advises anyone who has a weak immune system, or is pregnant, to ask a doctor before eating unpasteurised foods.
Probiotic pills contain living microbes, but the evidence for them is mixed. Some help with particular conditions, and a doctor or dietitian can say if you might need one.
Ines points to the label of a probiotic bottle, where a long name is followed by a short code. The code is the strain, and a strain that helps with one problem may do nothing for another.
Ines says that some strains have been shown in trials to help with certain problems, such as diarrhoea after antibiotics. The results differ from product to product, and none of them makes a miracle.

Ines warns that probiotics are not for everyone, and she says it twice. People with weak immune systems or serious illnesses should ask a doctor first, because rare but serious infections have been reported.

Ines tells Noah that supplements are not tested in the same way as medicines in many countries. The amount of live microbes on the label may not match what is inside, so a pharmacist can help with the choice.
Ines draws three boxes on a napkin to help Noah remember the long words. Probiotics are the microbes, prebiotics are the food that they eat, and postbiotics are the useful substances that they make.

Ines shows Noah an advertisement for a seven-day gut detox with dramatic before-and-after photographs. She teaches him the warning signs, such as no named strain, no trial and a promise to cure everything.
Noah decides to make his own sauerkraut, using a recipe from Dara. He washes a large jar, slices a cabbage, rubs it with salt and packs it down until the juice rises above the leaves.

By the third day the jar is full of tiny bubbles, and the cabbage has begun to smell pleasantly sour. Noah checks that the leaves stay under the liquid, because anything that rises to the surface can go bad.
After ten days Noah opens the jar and smells it carefully. Ines reminds him that a sour smell is normal, but fuzzy mould or a rotten smell means that the whole jar must be thrown away.
Mara has a bad chest infection, and her doctor gives her a course of antibiotics. After hearing so much from Noah about the gut, she phones him and asks whether she should refuse them.

Ines tells Noah to say one thing clearly to his sister, which is that antibiotics save lives. They also disturb gut microbes, so they should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them, and exactly as the doctor says.
Ines explains that antibiotics work against bacteria and not against viruses, so they do not help with colds or flu. Taking them when they are not needed also helps resistant bacteria to spread.
Ines says that after a course of antibiotics, the gut community usually begins to recover over the following weeks and months. For some people, a few changes may last longer than that.
Some people get loose stools while they take antibiotics, and it is usually mild. If it is severe or bloody, or comes with a fever or strong pain, they should speak to a doctor quickly.

Noah cooks a simple vegetable soup and takes it to Mara's flat with a banana and a tub of plain yoghurt. She is tired and weak, but she says that it is the nicest thing anyone has brought her all week.

Ines stops in an aisle of brightly coloured packets and explains what ultra-processed means. Such foods are made with ingredients and additives that are not found in a home kitchen, and they are usually low in fibre.
Ines says that some additives, such as emulsifiers, have changed gut microbes in animal studies. The evidence in people is limited and mixed, so nobody can say yet how much it matters.
Ines says that diets high in sugar and fat and low in fibre are linked with a less varied set of gut microbes. The link is real, but it does not prove that a slice of cake does damage by itself.
Noah and Tomasz sit on a bench and share a large slice of chocolate cake. Ines had told him that no food is a villain, and that a happy relationship with food matters as much as the fibre.
Ines tells Noah that sleep and stress both seem to affect the gut. The gut, in return, seems to affect sleep and stress, so the effects can go round in a circle.

Noah's working day is uneven, and he often eats late at night after a long shift. Ines says that irregular sleep and meals may disturb the body's daily rhythms, including those of the gut, although the research is early.
Ines advises Noah to avoid a heavy meal just before bed, because lying down soon after eating can cause heartburn. If heartburn happens often, he should talk to a doctor and not just buy tablets.

Ines suggests that Noah use his red lights for something other than eating, and teaches him a slow breathing exercise. He breathes in for four counts and out for six, and it makes the lights seem shorter.
Ines says that regular exercise is linked with a more varied gut community and with more regular bowel movements. Most of the studies are small, but the link has been found more than once.

Noah is already very active, and Ines points out that his main need is enough food and water to fuel his work. Fibre-rich foods fill the stomach, so he must make sure that he does not accidentally eat too little.
Fibre works best with enough fluid, and a lack of water, fibre and movement can cause constipation. Drinking regularly through the day is a simple habit.

Ines mentions other things that can help with constipation, such as not ignoring the urge to go and keeping a calm routine. Some medicines can also cause it, so a person who is unsure should ask a pharmacist.
Ines says that healthy bowel habits vary a great deal, from several times a day to a few times a week. What matters is what is normal for you, and any lasting change from that pattern.
Ines draws a circle with a tiny gut in the middle and five words around it. They are plants, water, movement, sleep and calm, and she says that none of them works alone.

Ines becomes serious and tells Noah to write down a list of warning signs, so he takes out his notebook. See a doctor, and not a diet book, for blood in the stool, black stools, weight loss, ongoing pain or a lasting change.
Ines explains that these warning signs can have many causes, and that most of them can be treated. Checking early is better than waiting, and it is never a waste of the doctor's time.

Ines mentions that many countries invite adults of a certain age to take part in bowel screening. She says that people should accept the invitation, because the test can find problems before any symptoms appear.

Tomasz quietly tells Noah that he has noticed blood on several occasions, and that he has been too embarrassed to see a doctor. Noah remembers the red list, and he helps his friend to book an appointment.
Tomasz sees Dr Ellis, who listens carefully, examines him and arranges some tests. The doctor finds a cause that can be treated, and says that he was right to come.
Ines introduces Noah to Hana, a registered dietitian at a community clinic. Hana explains that some people with bowel conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, need a personal plan.

Hana explains that for some people with irritable bowel syndrome, a dietitian may guide them through a short diet called low FODMAP. It has three steps, which are to cut out, to bring back and to personalise, and it is not meant to last for life.
Hana warns that anyone who suspects coeliac disease should have a test before they cut out gluten. If the person stops eating gluten first, the blood test may wrongly show that they are healthy.

Noah is tempted by an advertisement for a cleanse drink and a postal test kit that promise a personal diet. Hana says that the evidence for such products is weak, and that the body already clears its own waste.

Ines reminds Noah that a baby's microbes begin to form at birth, so a baby's diet should follow the advice of a doctor. Small children also need a balanced diet, because too much fibre can fill them up too quickly.
Noah's new breakfast is a bowl of porridge made with oats, topped with seeds, berries and a spoonful of plain yoghurt. It takes five minutes and keeps him full until the middle of the morning.
Noah packs a lunch of cold brown rice, mixed beans, chopped carrots and fresh herbs. It is cheap and easy to carry, and it also contains resistant starch.
Because the weather is getting warm, Noah buys a small insulated bag and a freezer block for his lunch. Ines reminds him that food which has been out in the heat for hours is not safe to eat.

For dinner Noah cooks a stew of lentils, carrots, onions and garlic, with Ines tasting from the side. Both onions and garlic contain prebiotic fibres, and the stew costs very little for four portions.
Noah makes a list of snacks that survive a day in a bicycle bag, such as fruit, nuts, a boiled egg and wholemeal bread. The egg stays in the cool bag, and he buys bananas at the fruit stall.
Noah goes out to a cafe with Tomasz and studies the menu carefully. He picks a dish with beans and vegetables, adds a side salad, and discovers that eating out can be gut-friendly too.
At the sandwich shop, Noah asks for a wholemeal roll with hummus, plenty of salad and a little cheese. It is not a perfect lunch, but it is far better than the plain white roll that he used to eat.
On a quiet Sunday Noah cooks a large pot of stew and divides it into containers. He cools it quickly, freezes most of it, and promises to reheat it until it is steaming hot.
Mara has recovered from her illness, and she comes to cook with Noah while Leo watches. She has started to hide lentils in the pasta sauce, and Leo eats his apple with the skin on.

At the end of the week, Noah counts thirty different plants and writes the number in large letters on the office whiteboard. The other couriers cheer, but Ines reminds him that it is a marker and not a prize.
Noah counts his coins at the end of the month and finds that he has spent less on food than before. Dried beans, oats, frozen vegetables, cabbage and carrots cost very little, and they fill him up.

After six weeks Noah knocks on Ines's door and tells her that he feels lighter, with more energy in the afternoons. She is glad, but says that everybody's results will differ and a feeling is not proof.
Ines writes a list of possible reasons on the whiteboard. The fibre may have helped, but so may the fewer crisps, the better sleep, the warmer weather and the attention that Noah has paid.
Noah turns through his notebook and sees some clear patterns. He has fewer afternoon dips, a calmer stomach and less wind than at the start, though the diary can show patterns and not proof.

Ines stands at the whiteboard, which is now covered with question marks around a drawing of the gut. She says that much about the microbiome is still unknown, and that good science means admitting what we do not know.

Ines tells Noah that the unknowns are what make the field exciting, because most of the research is only a few decades old. Careful trials are now under way, and honest scientists keep asking better questions.
Ines gives Noah five questions for reading health news. Was it done on people, how big was it, was it a trial, has anyone repeated it, and is someone selling something?
Noah decides how he will keep the new habits when the six weeks are over. He will add plants slowly, drink enough water, enjoy treats without guilt and ask a doctor when something is wrong.

To celebrate, Noah gives a thirty-plant dinner in his flat, and everyone brings a different plant. Ines, Kofi, Tomasz, Pavel and Mara fill the table with salads, beans, fruit and a jar of home-made sauerkraut.
This book is general information and is not medical advice. If you have a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy or a child to feed, ask a doctor or a registered dietitian first.
C1C2: Noah spends ten hours a day delivering parcels by bicycle, and he eats whatever is fastest, usually a sandwich or a bag of crisps at a red traffic light. Lately he has noticed that he feels heavy and sleepy in the afternoons, and he has started to wonder what all this hurried eating is doing inside his body. He decides that the person to ask is his neighbour Ines, who works at the university and always seems to know the answer.

The company dispatcher, a calm man called Pavel, sends a new delivery to Noah's phone every few minutes, and each one is marked urgent in a cheerful orange box. Noah crosses bridges, climbs stairs and waits in lobbies, and the day passes in a blur of doorbells and signatures. There is never a good moment to sit down, so lunch becomes whatever can be eaten with one hand and a red light.

Outside the post office, Noah's stomach produces a long, gurgling rumble that makes his friend Tomasz stop in the middle of a sentence. Tomasz, another courier who is never short of a joke, laughs and says that it sounds like a small motorbike waiting for the lights to change. Noah laughs too, but the noise has been happening every day for months, and he is beginning to find it a little less funny.

That evening Noah heaves his bicycle up four flights of stairs and meets his neighbour Ines on the third landing, fumbling for her keys. Her arms are full of a heavy shopping bag, and through the thin plastic he can see tins of beans, a bunch of onions and a great many green leaves. She works at the university, and he has long known that she studies something very small, though he has never quite understood what.

Standing on the landing with his helmet still in his hand, Noah finally asks the question that has been bothering him all week, which is what happens to a sandwich after he swallows it. Ines puts down her shopping bag, smiles broadly and says that he is not really asking about a body, but about a crowd. She adds that the crowd is so large and so busy that he will need more than one evening to meet it.

Ines offers Noah a deal there on the landing, which is that she will explain what she knows over the next six weeks if he is willing to try a few small changes to his meals. Her only condition is that he accepts three words that scientists use more often than anyone admits, namely I do not know. Noah, who has never been promised an honest answer before, shakes her hand at once.

On Saturday morning Noah locks his bicycle to a railing outside the university and follows Ines through a maze of corridors that smell faintly of soap and warm machinery. Every glass door carries a small sign with a long, unpronounceable name, and behind them people in white coats are bending over benches in a strange and absorbing silence. He feels like a visitor to another country, a place where everyone is speaking in whispers.

Ines's student Kofi spreads a tiny drop of plain yoghurt on a glass slide, slides it under a microscope and invites Noah to look through the eyepiece. At first he sees only a smear of grey, but as the focus sharpens a crowd of minute rods and chains appears, thousands of them, drifting and crowding together. Kofi says that these are the microbes that turn milk into yoghurt, and Noah, who has eaten yoghurt for years, feels strangely as though he has been introduced to his lunch.

Before he leaves, Ines hands Noah a small green notebook and explains the three rules that will govern the next six weeks. He must be curious enough to ask questions, careful enough to check what he is told, and patient enough to change his habits slowly rather than all at once. She laughs when he asks whether there will be an exam, and says that his own body will be the only examiner.

Outside in the pale afternoon sun, Noah sits on a bench beside his bicycle, opens the green notebook and writes the date at the top of the first page. Beneath it, in large and slightly crooked letters, he writes a single question, which is what actually happens to my lunch after I swallow it. It feels like the beginning of something, and for the first time in months he is not thinking about the next delivery at all.

On Sunday morning, with a cup of tea at her elbow, Ines draws a long and winding tube across the whiteboard that hangs in her kitchen. She explains that the gut runs from the mouth all the way to the end of the body, and that if it were stretched out straight it would be several metres long. Noah looks at the loops and coils and says that it looks like a plate of spaghetti.

Ines hands Noah a plain, dry cracker and asks him to chew it for a full minute without swallowing. To his surprise it slowly begins to taste sweet, because an ingredient in his saliva has started to break the starch into simple sugars before the food has even left his mouth. She says that digestion begins with the first bite, and that this is one good reason not to swallow lunch in three seconds at a red light.

Once the food is swallowed, it does not simply drop down the throat like a stone down a well. Rings of muscle in the gullet squeeze it along in slow, rhythmic waves, and it is the same movement that carries food through the rest of the gut. This is why a person can swallow a drink while standing on their head, as Tomasz once demonstrated, much to the alarm of a nearby waiter.

The stomach is a muscular, stretchy bag that churns the food and mixes it with a strong acid, rather like a washing machine filled with lemon juice. The acid kills many of the microbes that arrive with a meal, which is one of the body's first lines of defence, and the food usually stays there for a few hours before moving on. Noah says that he has never felt anything so hard-working, and Ines tells him that he has not even met the clever part yet.

Beyond the stomach lies the small intestine, a long and narrow tube in which most of the food is broken down into pieces small enough to pass into the blood. Its inner wall is covered in tiny folds and finger-like bumps called villi, and together they give the gut a surface far larger than anyone would guess from the outside. Noah says that it sounds like a very busy shop, and Ines says that it is more like an airport.

The gut does not work alone, and Ines draws two helpers beside the tube, using a green marker for the liver and a yellow one for the pancreas. The liver makes a liquid called bile, which is stored in the gall bladder and helps the body to deal with fats, while the pancreas sends juices that break down starch, fat and protein. Noah copies the drawing carefully into his notebook and decides to call it the kitchen staff.

Not everything in a meal can be broken down by the body's own juices, and Ines draws a thick arrow to show where the leftovers go. The parts that human digestion cannot manage, which are mostly fibre, continue on their journey into the final section of the tube, and she taps the arrow twice with her marker. Noah asks whether leftovers are wasted, and she smiles and tells him that they are the most interesting part of the whole story.
