The large intestine is shorter than the small one but a good deal wider, and Ines draws it curving around the edge of the whiteboard like a frame around a picture. Its main jobs are to take water back from what remains of the meal and to prepare the rest for leaving the body, and it is also the home of most of the gut's microbes. Noah leans closer to the drawing, because this is the first time that she has mentioned residents.

Ines explains that the whole journey, from the first bite to the end of the tube, often takes a day or two, although it varies a great deal from one person to the next. She adds that sweetcorn is a famous way to see this for oneself, because the tough yellow skins are fibre that human digestion cannot break down and so they pass through almost unchanged. Noah looks down at his plate and decides that he will postpone this particular experiment until after lunch.

Ines tells Noah something that surprises him, which is that the inside of the gut is, in a sense, still outside the body, like the hole through a doughnut. Its thin lining, protected by a layer of slippery mucus, acts as a careful gate that lets in the useful pieces of food and keeps out germs and anything harmful. Noah writes in his notebook that his lunch has not truly entered him until the gate has agreed, and Ines says that this is as good a summary as any textbook could give.

Ines picks up a blue marker and fills the large intestine on her drawing with a dense crowd of tiny dots, packed together like people on a rush-hour train. She says that this is where most of the gut's microbes live, and that by recent estimates the body holds about as many microbes as it does human cells, although nobody can count them exactly. Noah looks down at his own stomach with a new feeling of respect and a little suspicion.

Ines writes the word microbe on the whiteboard and draws a circle around it, because she says that everything else in the book depends on this one idea. A microbe is a living thing so small that it can be seen only through a microscope, and most of the ones in the gut are bacteria, although there are fungi and viruses in the mix as well. Noah, who had always assumed that a microbe was simply a germ, admits that the word has changed its meaning in his mind.

Kofi pulls a single hair from the top of Noah's head, with a quick apology, and lays it on the microscope stage beside a picture of gut bacteria drawn to the same scale. Dozens of the bacteria could be lined up side by side across the width of that one hair, and he explains that this is why nobody suspected their existence until microscopes became powerful enough, a few centuries ago. Noah rubs the sore spot on his scalp and says that the lesson was convincing.

Ines holds up a jar of thick green soup with the word Microbiome written across the label, and says that this is the best image she can offer. The microbiome is the whole community of microbes that live in and on a person, and like a soup it contains many different ingredients in different amounts, so that no two people share exactly the same recipe. Noah asks whether he is allowed to taste it, and she tells him firmly that it is only pea soup.

A single healthy gut can hold hundreds of different kinds of microbe, and Ines fills a corner of the whiteboard with their long Latin names in a dozen colours. Two people share many of the same ones, in the way that two cities share many of the same shops, but each person's own mix is slightly different, and it changes over time. Noah looks at the list and says that he hopes none of them is called Noah, and Ines laughs until she has to sit down.

A baby begins life with very few microbes inside, and the first ones arrive during birth and from milk, from skin and from the surroundings of the new home. Over the first few years of life the community grows richer and more varied, and it slowly begins to look more like an adult's, although scientists are still working out how much each early influence matters. Noah thinks of his sister's small son and wonders how many visitors have already moved in.

Ines reminds Noah that the gut is only one of the places where microbes live, because the mouth, the skin and several other parts of the body each have their own communities, quite different from one another. The community on a tooth is not the same as the one on an elbow, and neither of them resembles the crowd in the colon, which is a good reason to keep brushing the teeth twice a day. Noah promises that he will, though he cannot resist asking whether the mouth microbes ever get lonely.

Many of the microbes that live in the large intestine have adapted to a place with almost no oxygen, and fresh air can harm or even kill them. To grow them in the laboratory, scientists keep them in sealed cabinets without oxygen, and Kofi works through thick rubber gloves fixed to the front panel, like a person washing dishes in a very strange sink. Noah says that he has never seen anyone look so calm while handling a crowd of invisible neighbours.

Because many gut microbes are fussy and have never been persuaded to grow in a dish, scientists now identify them by reading the genetic material, or DNA, that they leave in a sample. Ines shows Noah a computer screen full of long strings of coloured letters, each one a clue to a microbe, and explains that this method has changed the whole field in the last few decades. Noah looks at the scrolling letters and admits that detective work has never looked so colourful.

On the tram home that evening, Noah opens his notebook and writes in large capital letters that he is never eating alone. He thinks about the great invisible crowd in the dark of the large intestine, going about its business, and for the first time in his life he wonders what it would like for dinner. It is a strange question, but he finds that he is looking forward to the answer.

Ines tells Noah that the word germ has given microbes a bad name, because the great majority of them are harmless and many are genuinely helpful, and only a few cause disease. A large and varied crowd can also make life difficult for the troublemakers, since they must compete for space and food with residents that are already well settled. Noah says that the gut sounds like a crowded bus that has no seat for strangers.

Ines draws a bus that is already full of friendly passengers, with a small spiky germ left on the pavement outside, shaking its fist. It is a simple picture of how the gut's own microbes compete with newcomers for food and for space, and sometimes they even make substances that slow the newcomers down. Noah says that he would like to meet the driver, and Ines says that in truth there is no driver at all, only a lot of passengers who get on.

Ines is quick to add that harmful germs certainly do exist, and that they can cause food poisoning, with symptoms that no one wishes to describe over breakfast. Washing the hands before eating, cooking meat all the way through, keeping raw and cooked food apart and storing food in a cold fridge are all simple habits that keep the troublemakers away. Noah realises that being friendly to gut microbes does not mean being careless about hygiene.

The first job of the gut's microbes, Ines explains, is to help with digestion, particularly of the plant foods that the body's own juices have no power to break down. In return for the work, the microbes receive a meal, and the arrangement is so old and so successful that neither side could easily do without the other. Noah says that this is the best deal that he has ever heard of, and certainly better than his contract at the courier company.

A second job is to make a few vitamins, and Ines mentions vitamin K and several of the B vitamins as examples that gut microbes are known to produce. She is careful to add that most of the vitamins that a person needs still come from food, and that scientists are still working out how much of the microbial supply the body actually absorbs. Noah, who had been about to cancel his multivitamin in a burst of enthusiasm, puts the thought quietly away.

A large share of the body's immune system sits close to the gut, which makes sense, since the gut is the place where the body meets the greatest number of foreign things in the shortest time. Early in life, the resident microbes seem to help the immune system to learn which visitors are friends and which are enemies, and a calm and well-trained defence is better than a jumpy one. Ines says that this training is one of the most exciting areas of research, and that it is also one of the least settled.

Kofi shows Noah a chart that follows the gut from one end to the other, and the line that represents the number of microbes climbs steeply as it goes. There are very few in the acid of the stomach, a modest number in the small intestine, and by far the greatest crowd in the large intestine, where food moves slowly and there is little oxygen. Noah says that the gut seems to have its own neighbourhoods, some quiet and some packed.

Noah asks Ines what a perfect microbiome looks like, hoping to copy it, and she answers that nobody really knows. Healthy people carry many different mixes of microbes, so scientists look for patterns, such as variety and stability, rather than for a single ideal that every person ought to match. It is the first time that she says I do not know, and Noah, rather to his own surprise, finds that he trusts her more because of it.

Tomasz, who is rather afraid of germs, cleans his handlebars with hand gel every hour and offers a squirt to anyone who passes. Ines says that washing the hands at the right moments is sensible, for instance before eating and after the toilet. There is no need to fight every microbe in daily life, she adds, and no way to win if one tried, and Noah relays this to Tomasz, who takes it as a personal insult.

Ines tells Noah that, in her opinion, it is more helpful to think of the gut as a garden to be tended than as a battlefield to be won. Its microbes do three important jobs, which are digesting what the body cannot, making a few vitamins and training the immune system, and they do them best when they are well fed and not disturbed too often. Noah draws a small garden in his notebook and, after some thought, adds a very small bicycle.

Before an important delivery to a large and rather frightening office, Noah feels a fluttering sensation in his stomach that has nothing to do with lunch. He has noticed the same thing before exams, interviews and one memorable first date, and later that evening he asks Ines why a feeling that starts in the head can be felt so clearly in the belly. She says that it is the best question that he has asked so far.

The gut and the brain are in constant conversation, sending messages along nerves and through hormones and immune signals. Scientists are studying whether gut microbes can influence mood, stress and sleep, and the early results are fascinating, but most of them come from animals or small studies and cannot yet be turned into advice. Ines says that she would love to tell him more, but she would rather be honest than exciting.

Ines draws a long, looping line from the brain down through the neck and into the belly, and she explains that this is the vagus nerve, one of the main cables between the two. Surprisingly, a good share of the messages that travel along it go upward, from the gut to the brain, so that the belly is as much a speaker as a listener. Noah says that this finally explains why his own stomach seems to have so many strong opinions.

The wall of the gut contains a network of nerve cells of its own, hundreds of millions of them, which can manage much of the work of digestion without waiting for orders from the brain. It is sometimes called the second brain, although Ines points out that it neither thinks nor feels in the way that the brain does, and that the nickname is more poetic than precise. Noah copies down the word enteric into his notebook and promises himself that he will use it at the next party.

As food passes through the gut, cells in its lining release hormones that travel to the brain with the message that the body is beginning to feel full. The message takes a little while to arrive, which is why a person who eats in five minutes standing next to a bicycle can easily finish a meal without ever feeling that it has been enough. Noah suddenly understands why he is hungry again at three o'clock, and decides to sit down for his next lunch.

Kofi explains that scientists have raised special mice that have no gut microbes at all, and that these animals respond to stress and behave quite differently from ordinary mice. The experiments suggest that microbes can influence the brain in some way, but Kofi stresses that a mouse is not a person, and that many results from animals have failed to carry over to humans. Noah, who has been getting rather excited, writes mice in capital letters and underlines it twice.

Several small studies have tested probiotics on people with low mood or anxiety, and the results so far are mixed, with some showing a small benefit and others showing none at all. Ines is firm that nobody should try to treat a serious mood problem with yoghurt, however fine the yoghurt may be, and that a person who feels low or anxious for a long time should talk to a doctor. Noah nods slowly, because he has a friend who needs to hear this sentence.

Stress can upset the gut in ways that many people recognise, such as cramps or loose stools before an exam or a big event, because the nerves and hormones that carry the stress signal also reach the belly. Ines wants Noah to understand that the pain is real even when stress is part of the cause, and that nobody should ever be told that it is merely imaginary. Noah thinks of a cousin who was once told exactly that by a stranger, and he feels a small flash of anger.

Ines suggests that Noah keep a very simple diary for a week, noting down what he eats, when he eats it and how he feels afterwards, with a happy face, a tired face or a hungry one. She warns him that a diary can reveal patterns but can never prove that one thing causes another, since sleep, weather and traffic all have their own opinions. Noah starts the diary that night with a rather bleak and guilty entry about crisps.

Ines warns Noah that many internet claims about the gut and the brain run far ahead of the science, and that anyone who promises a happier mind through a single food should be treated with suspicion. Her own advice is modest and practical, which is to eat regular meals, enjoy a wide variety of foods, sleep well and be patient with a body that changes slowly. Noah closes his notebook, a little disappointed but a good deal wiser, and goes to find something to eat.

The microbes of the large intestine have to eat like everyone else, and their meals are the leftovers that the body has been unable to digest on its own. Most of this leftover food is fibre, and Ines says that when a person chooses what to eat, they are also, whether they know it or not, choosing the menu for a crowd of trillions. Noah says that he has never before been responsible for such a large number of guests.

Fibre is the part of plant foods that human digestion cannot break down, and it comes in several different kinds with different properties. Ines lays out a stalk of wheat, a carrot and an apple on the kitchen table to show where some of it hides, and she explains that it forms the walls, skins and stems that hold plants together. Noah picks up the carrot and says that he has been eating furniture all his life.

Ines explains that fibre is not a single substance at all but a large family of them, each with its own structure. Leaves and stems contain cellulose, apples and many other fruits contain a substance called pectin, and oats contain beta-glucan, and different microbes in the gut prefer different members of the family. Noah, who had thought of fibre as a kind of brown dust, begins to feel that he has insulted an entire dynasty.

Soluble fibre mixes with water and forms a soft, sticky gel, as when oats thicken into porridge in a pan, while insoluble fibre does not dissolve and instead adds bulk and roughness to what passes through the gut. Most plant foods contain a mixture of both kinds, in different proportions, so there is no need to count them separately. Noah says that this is a relief, since he can hardly keep count of the parcels in his bag.

Ines points out something that Noah had never thought about, which is that meat, fish, eggs and dairy foods contain no fibre at all, so all of it comes from plants. These animal foods have other virtues, but a sandwich of ham and cheese on white bread offers the crowd in the large intestine very little to eat. Noah looks at his usual lunch with the guilty expression of a man who has forgotten to feed the cat.

On Saturday, Ines takes Noah to a supermarket and stops in front of the long aisle of bread, where dozens of loaves offer very different promises. White flour has had much of the outer layer of the grain removed, which makes it softer but leaves less fibre, whereas wholemeal and wholegrain breads keep more of it. She tells him that a brown colour alone proves nothing, so he should read the label.

Ines shows Noah how to read the back of the packet, beginning with the list of ingredients, in which the first item named is always the largest. She adds that in many countries a food with about six grams of fibre in every hundred grams may be called high in fibre. The exact rules differ from place to place, and Noah finds that his usual white loaf scores very poorly, and he puts it back with an apology.

Ines tells Noah that fibre does a good deal more than feed microbes, since it also helps a person to feel full for longer and keeps the bowels moving. Soluble fibre, such as the beta-glucan in oats and barley, may help to steady blood sugar after a meal and to lower cholesterol. Several large studies link diets that are rich in fibre with a lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, and she reminds him, as always, that a link is not the same as proof.

Noah wonders whether he could simply buy a tub of fibre powder and stir a spoonful into his morning coffee, and he is almost proud of the idea. Ines says that whole plant foods bring many kinds of fibre together with vitamins, minerals and other useful substances, which no single powder can match, although some people with particular needs are advised by a doctor to use a supplement. Noah puts the tub back on the shelf and picks up a bag of beans instead.

Noah buys a bag of oats and a bag of dried lentils, his first purchases for what he is beginning to call the project, and carries them proudly out of the supermarket. On the way home he asks Ines how a microbe can possibly eat, since it has no mouth, no teeth and certainly no knife and fork. She says that she has been waiting for him to ask, and that the answer involves bubbles.

Ines explains that gut microbes eat fibre by fermenting it, which simply means breaking it down in a place where there is almost no oxygen. It is the same family of processes that makes bread dough rise in a warm kitchen and turns milk into yoghurt, and Noah realises that he has been living with fermentation all his life without once giving it a thought. She tells him that the large intestine is, in a sense, a very long and very patient bakery.

When microbes ferment fibre, one of the main things they make is a group of substances called short-chain fatty acids, and Ines writes the long name on the whiteboard in a confident green. These substances feed the cells that line the large intestine and may help to calm inflammation, which is one reason why scientists are so interested in them. Noah writes the name in his notebook, crosses it out, and writes SCFAs in much smaller letters.

One of these acids is called butyrate, and Ines explains that the cells lining the colon use it as one of their favourite fuels, taking a large share of their energy from it. In other words, the gut's own cells depend on a meal that is cooked by microbes, and the quality of that meal depends on what the person has eaten. Noah says that this is a very long and complicated way to get dinner.

A small amount of these acids passes through the wall of the gut into the blood, and from there it travels around the body to other organs. Researchers think that it may affect appetite, blood sugar and even the way that fat is stored, although much of the evidence comes from laboratory and animal studies, and the picture in real people is still incomplete. Ines says that the sentence that scientists use most often is that more research is needed, and that for once it is true.

Fermentation makes gas, so a little wind is simply the sound of the microbes at work, and Ines announces this fact in the same calm voice that she uses for everything else. Most healthy people pass wind many times a day, whether they admit it or not, and a gut that never produced any would be a gut with very hungry microbes. Noah tries not to laugh in the middle of the laboratory corridor, and fails.

Most of the gas in the gut, Ines explains, is hydrogen and carbon dioxide, which have no smell at all. The unpleasant smell comes from tiny amounts of gases that contain sulphur, made when microbes break down foods such as eggs, meat, onions and cabbage. A strong smell on its own is not a sign of illness, and it says more about the dinner than about the health, so Noah resolves to avoid cabbage on days when he delivers to the library.

Kofi mixes warm water, a spoonful of sugar and a pinch of dried yeast in a clean bottle, and stretches a balloon over the neck. After half an hour the balloon begins to swell slowly, because yeast, which is a kind of fungus, ferments the sugar and releases gas. He says that this is not the same as the gut, but that it shows the idea, and Noah watches the balloon grow with the delight of a child.

Ines describes how the microbes of the gut often work in teams, because the waste produced by one kind can become a meal for another. Together they form a long chain, rather like the workers on a factory line, that breaks down fibre step by step until almost nothing is left. Noah says that this is the most efficient recycling system he has ever heard of, and certainly better than the one in his building.

Not every microbe can digest every kind of fibre, so each kind of fibre tends to feed its own particular group, in the way that different crops support different animals on a farm. A diet that offers a wide range of fibres therefore tends to support a larger and more varied community of microbes, which becomes one of the main themes of the weeks ahead. Noah, who has so far eaten about three kinds of plant a week, feels a little embarrassed.

That night Noah writes a short and slightly embarrassing thank-you note to his microbes in the back of his notebook, and decides that he will feed them a great deal more fibre from tomorrow. Ines, who happens to pass his open door and reads the note over his shoulder, warns him that the amount matters. A sudden flood of fibre is not a kindness to a gut that is not used to it, she says, and Noah, who had been planning a great feast of beans, reluctantly puts down his spoon.

Ines tells Noah that many national health guides advise adults to eat about thirty grams of fibre a day, and she writes the number on the whiteboard in a large, serious circle. Most adults eat less than that, and in many countries the average is far below it, which means that Noah is in very good, if not very healthy, company. He asks how much thirty grams is, and she says that it is smaller than he thinks and harder than he expects.

Ines writes out a sample day of meals that could come close to thirty grams of fibre, and Noah copies it into his notebook. It begins with porridge and fruit, continues with a wholemeal sandwich, an apple with its skin and a bean stew, and ends with a handful of nuts, and the grams add up gradually rather than all at once. He notices that nothing on the list is strange or expensive, which strikes him as an unfair surprise.

For three days Noah writes down everything that he eats, and each evening he looks up the fibre in each item on the packets and in the table that Ines has lent him. His usual average comes to about eleven grams a day, which is less than half of what the guides suggest, and the largest contribution comes from a single apple that he ate by accident. He shows the notebook to Ines, who is kind enough to look serious rather than amused.

Ines explains why so many adults fall short of the target, and the reasons turn out to be quite ordinary. Many of the foods that fill a modern shopping basket, such as white bread, biscuits and ready meals, have lost their fibre in processing or never had much, and busy people reach for them. Noah says that it is not his fault, and Ines agrees, which is a pleasant surprise.

Ines shows Noah that the guides of different countries suggest slightly different amounts of fibre, often somewhere between about twenty-five and thirty-eight grams a day depending on age and sex. Children need less than adults, so a parent should check the guidance for their child's age, and the number is best treated as a direction of travel and not as an examination that can be failed. Noah tears out the page from the notebook where he had drawn a large cross.

Ines adds an important warning to the thirty-gram target, which she says applies to healthy adults and not to everyone. A few people are advised by their doctors to eat less fibre for a time, for example after certain bowel operations or during a flare of some bowel conditions, and they should follow that advice and not a general guide. Noah underlines the word everyone in his notebook, with a pen that is nearly empty.

Ines suggests swaps in place of a total revolution, because it is easier to change what one already eats than to learn a whole new way of cooking. Wholemeal bread can replace white bread, brown rice can replace white rice, and plain popcorn, which is in fact a whole grain, can replace a bag of crisps at the red light. Noah, who had never suspected that his favourite cinema snack was healthy, looks at it with new suspicion.

Tomasz finds Noah sitting on the kerb eating a bag of plain popcorn instead of his usual crisps, and he teases him loudly about becoming a health fanatic. Within a minute, however, he is asking for a handful, and then another, and he admits grudgingly that it is a good deal less greasy than the thing he usually eats. Noah says that this is how revolutions begin, with one small act of snacking.

Some packaged foods, such as snack bars and drinks, have fibre added to them, often in the form of a powder made from a plant root, and the label announces it proudly in large letters. Ines says that these products are not wicked, and that they can be useful, but that whole foods offer more than fibre alone, since they bring vitamins, minerals and a variety of other substances in the same package. Noah puts the chocolate bar back, although he looks at it for some time.

That evening Noah draws a small ladder on a sheet of paper, with one rung for each week, and sticks it to the door of his fridge. The plan is to add a little more fibre every few days, to drink plenty of water and to notice how his body responds, and the first rung says only add one apple. Ines, who has been invited to inspect it, says that it is the most sensible plan that anyone has shown her all year.

On Monday morning Ines reminds Noah of the golden rule of the whole project, which is that fibre must be added slowly, over a period of weeks, and with plenty of water. A gut that has been used to very little for years needs time to adjust, and so do the microbes that live in it, and she tells him to be patient. Noah, who is not a patient man before breakfast, promises that he will try.

Noah, who has never done anything by halves, ignores the advice and cooks an enormous pot of bean chilli on the very first evening. He eats two large bowls with great enthusiasm, and by midnight his stomach is tight and round and gurgling like a kettle, so that he lies awake listening to his own insides. He resolves, rather stiffly, that Ines was right and that he will begin again tomorrow with a spoonful.

Ines explains over the wall the next morning that the microbes in his gut need time to multiply and learn the new menu, and that the gut muscles and nerves need time to adjust to the extra bulk. A sudden change allows neither of them any time at all, whereas a small change every few days lets the whole system keep up. Noah says that he understands completely, and she says that she could hear this the night before.

Beans and lentils are among the richest sources of fibre in the kitchen, and Ines tells Noah to begin with just two or three spoonfuls on the side of his plate. She also suggests rinsing tinned beans in a colander under the tap, which washes away some of the sugars in the liquid that microbes turn into gas, and she demonstrates with a tin that makes a pleasing rattle. Noah rinses the next tin with great ceremony, counting the seconds under the tap like a surgeon who is washing his hands before an operation.

Ines gives Noah a serious warning about dried beans, which is that they must be soaked overnight, drained and then cooked until they are fully soft. Raw or undercooked red kidney beans contain a natural poison that can make a person quite ill. The usual advice is to boil them hard for at least ten minutes, because a slow cooker alone may not get hot enough, and Noah sticks a note with the number ten on the front of his cooker.

Lentils need no soaking and cook in about twenty minutes, which makes them an ideal ingredient for a cyclist with no spare evenings. Noah makes a simple soup of red lentils, carrots and onions, and watches with delight as the little orange discs soften and melt into a thick, golden broth. It tastes better than anything that he has made so far, and he eats only a small bowl, exactly as he had agreed to do.

Noah makes a small chart on the kitchen wall to record how much wind he has each day, using a scale of one to five that is entirely his own invention. The numbers are high in the first week, with a worrying peak on the day of the chilli, but by the second week they begin to drop as his gut and his microbes adapt to the new menu. Ines examines the chart with the solemn face of a doctor, and he realises that she is trying not to laugh.

At the courier office, Noah shares a tub of his lentil soup with Pavel and Tomasz, who taste it carefully, as men do when they expect to be disappointed. Pavel asks for the recipe, which is simple enough to be written on a napkin, and within a week half the office is talking about beans, lentils and the price of tinned tomatoes. Noah reflects that he has become the unofficial dietitian of a company that delivers parcels.

Ines tells Noah that a little extra wind and fullness are normal while the gut adjusts, but she is careful to draw a line between discomfort and a warning sign. If there is real pain, or the symptoms are severe or do not settle after a few weeks, he should step back to a smaller amount of fibre and speak to a doctor, rather than trying to push through. Noah thanks her for saying so plainly, because he is the kind of man who often pushes through.

After two weeks of small steps, Noah is eating noticeably more fibre and drinking a good deal more water, and his stomach has become calmer and a great deal quieter. He has not turned into a new person, and he is careful to say so to anyone who asks, but he notices that his afternoons are a little less heavy than before. He writes the date in his notebook and puts a small, cautious tick beside it.

Ines moves on to grains, and lines up jars of oats, pearl barley and brown rice along the kitchen counter like a small and well-behaved army. Whole grains keep the outer layers where most of the fibre is found, and oats and barley also contain beta-glucan, the soft, gel-forming fibre that she mentioned earlier. Noah says that he has walked past these jars in the shop a thousand times without suspecting that they were important.

Ines draws a grain of wheat and splits it into three coloured layers, which are the bran on the outside, the germ at the heart and the starchy centre. Refining removes the bran and the germ, which are the parts that hold most of the fibre and many of the vitamins and minerals, and leaves mostly starch. Noah says that it seems a strange way to treat a perfectly good seed, and she says that white flour keeps better and tastes softer, which is why it became so popular.

Noah makes his first pot of porridge on Tuesday morning, and it comes out so thick that his spoon can stand upright in the middle without any help. After some experiments with more water, a pinch of salt and a sliced banana instead of his usual spoonful of sugar, he arrives at a version that is creamy, warm and filling, and he is rather proud of it. He photographs it and sends the picture to his sister, who replies with a single astonished question mark.

Ines shows Noah an even wider world of grains and seeds, such as rye, buckwheat, quinoa and barley, and explains that each one brings a different mix of fibres to the table. Pearl barley is cheap, keeps for months in a cupboard and is excellent in soups and stews, so it becomes a favourite of the project at once. Noah adds a handful to his next pot of lentils and is astonished at how plump and chewy it becomes.

Fruit and vegetables bring a good deal of fibre as well, and the skins of many of them contain more of it than the soft flesh inside. Provided that the skins are washed thoroughly, Noah can eat apples, pears, carrots and potatoes without peeling them, and he finds that this saves time as well as adding fibre. Ines points out that different fruits and vegetables feed different microbes, which is another reason to choose them in great variety.

Ines tells Noah that frozen vegetables keep their fibre and are usually frozen soon after they are picked, so that they hold on to their goodness for months. They are cheap, they never go off in the bottom of the fridge, and they are ready in minutes, which suits a courier who has no time to chop and a bad record with lettuce. Noah fills his freezer with peas, spinach and mixed vegetables that very afternoon, feeling unusually organised.

Chickpeas belong to the same family of pulses as beans and lentils, and they are cheap, filling and rich in fibre, with a gentle nutty taste. Noah learns to blend a tin of them with lemon juice, a little garlic and a spoonful of tahini into a creamy hummus, and he packs it with carrot sticks in his bicycle bag. Tomasz, passing by, tries a spoonful and announces that he would like to place a regular order.

Nuts and seeds add fibre and healthy fats to a meal, and Noah begins to sprinkle a spoonful of chopped walnuts and seeds over his morning porridge. Whole flax seeds often pass through the gut unchanged, so it is better to use them ground, and chia seeds should be soaked. Nuts can be dangerous for anyone with an allergy, and food labels in many countries must warn about them, while Ines reminds him that a handful is a good portion, because nuts are also rich in energy.

Ines gives Noah a rule of thumb that he finds easy to remember, which is that the closer a food is to the plant that it came from, the more of its fibre it is likely to keep. A whole orange, for instance, has much more fibre than a glass of its juice, and it fills the stomach for far longer, because the juicing process takes most of the fibre away. Noah drinks his juice slowly, in the manner of a man who feels that he has been caught.

By the end of the week Noah's notebook shows that his fibre has climbed to about twenty grams a day, nearly double his starting point, and the fridge behind him is full of vegetables, jars and half-eaten fruit. Ines is pleased with him, and she says that the next step is not simply more fibre but more variety, because the microbes want a menu and not just a mountain of one thing. Noah is not sure what this means, but he is eager to find out.

Ines hands Noah a long list of plant foods, each one written in a different colour, from artichokes and apples to walnuts and watercress. She explains that variety matters at least as much as quantity, because different microbes like different fibres, and a varied diet feeds a more varied community. Noah studies the list for a long time and discovers that he has eaten fewer than a dozen of them in the last month.

Ines shows Noah a large citizen-science survey in which thousands of volunteers recorded what they ate and sent in samples so that their gut microbes could be studied. The people who ate more than thirty different kinds of plant a week had, on average, a more varied community of microbes than those who ate ten or fewer, although Ines warns that this is a link and not proof. Noah, who is now keeping score of everything, writes thirty in his notebook and underlines it.

Ines explains with a cheerful drawing why a link is not the same as proof, putting an ice cream beside a sunburned nose on the whiteboard. Sales of ice cream and cases of sunburn rise together in summer, but it is the sun that causes both. In the same way, people who eat thirty plants a week may also exercise more, sleep better or have more money, and Noah says that scientists must find the world very complicated, which she admits is true.

Ines explains that every distinct kind of plant food counts toward the weekly total, including fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds, beans, whole grains, herbs and spices, and that a tin of mixed beans counts as several. The figure of thirty is simply the marker that the researchers used in one survey, and it is not a magic number below which a person fails. Noah, who loves a clear rule, is faintly disappointed to hear this, and he looks at his chart again.

Noah sticks a chart to his fridge and puts a tick next to every kind of plant that he eats during the week. Herbs, spices, nuts, seeds, beans and grains all count, and so a tin of mixed beans, a pinch of cumin and a handful of walnuts quickly push his score upwards. By the end of the first week he has reached twelve, which is double what he had eaten the week before.

Noah discovers that mixed bags are the laziest and most effective way to raise his score, and he walks around the supermarket filling his basket with them. A tin of mixed beans, a packet of mixed seeds, a bag of frozen stir-fry vegetables and a box of mixed salad leaves each bring several different plants into a single meal. Ines, when she sees his full basket, says that she has never been so proud of a shopping list in her life.

On Saturday Noah visits the street market near his flat, where he has walked past the stalls a hundred times, and he buys a large, knobbly vegetable that he cannot name. The woman behind the stall, who has sold him nothing before, tells him how to peel and roast it, and he adds a new plant to the chart with the pride of a man who has discovered an island. He later learns that it is a celeriac, which is hardly a rarity, and that half the street has been cooking it for years.

Herbs and spices count as plants, and Noah begins to cook with cumin, paprika, parsley, coriander and mint, enjoying the smell that fills the whole flat. Ines is honest that a pinch adds very little fibre, so the benefit is probably small in itself, but the flavour makes beans and vegetables so appetising that he eats far more of them than he ever did. Noah says that this is the most delicious piece of science that he has been taught.

Tomasz hears about the fridge chart and challenges Noah to a contest to see who can eat the largest number of different plants in a single week, with the loser paying for the coffee. Pavel, who cannot resist an organised competition, draws a scoreboard on the office whiteboard, and within two days five couriers are counting herbs, beans and the toppings on their pizzas. Noah wonders, with a mixture of pride and alarm, whether Ines has accidentally started a small movement.

Noah finishes the week with twenty-two different plants and wins the contest by a single point, to the loud complaints of Tomasz. Ines congratulates him, but she reminds him that thirty is a marker and not an exam, and that people with bowel conditions or allergies may need personal advice about which plants they can eat comfortably. Noah says that he will keep the chart for as long as it is fun, and promises that it will always be a game and never a burden.

Ines draws a rainforest crowded with different trees, birds and insects beside a bare field in which only one crop grows, and she asks Noah which of them he would trust in a storm. A varied gut community is a little like the rainforest, because a mixture of microbes is generally linked with better health and greater resilience, while a narrow one is more easily knocked down. Noah says that he would like a gut like a jungle, and Ines says that this is an unusual thing to wish for.

Ines warns Noah that diversity is a useful clue about the state of the gut, but that it is not a score to be chased like a prize. A very high number does not always mean better health, and nobody can say what the ideal number would be, so the figure on a test result is a good deal less important than the habits that lie behind it. Noah, who had been planning to compete, quietly crosses a line out of his notebook.

Ines explains that a varied community of gut microbes seems to recover better after a disturbance, such as an illness, a stressful month or a course of antibiotics, because there are more species on hand to fill the gaps. Researchers are still collecting evidence in people, but the idea fits what ecologists have long observed in forests, lakes and meadows. Noah says that he finds it comforting to think of his gut as a small piece of nature.

Ines tells Noah about studies of traditional communities, such as the Hadza in Tanzania, who gather wild plants, honey and fruit as part of their daily food. Their gut microbes were found to be more varied than those of many city dwellers, although their lives differ in countless other ways, from the amount of walking to the water that they drink, so the comparison needs care. Noah says that he cycles forty miles a day, and she tells him that this does not make him a hunter-gatherer.

Ines introduces a new word, prebiotics, which she defines as fibres that selectively feed the microbes that are thought to be helpful, and she lays out garlic, leeks, onions and asparagus on the chopping board. Oats and slightly green bananas, which are firm and not yet sweet, contain prebiotic fibres as well, and none of these foods is exotic or expensive. Noah says that the prebiotic shelf of any supermarket is evidently the vegetable aisle.

One of the best-known prebiotic fibres is called inulin, and it is found in onions, garlic, leeks, chicory root and several other plants that Noah has never cooked. Jerusalem artichokes are particularly rich in it, and they are famous for causing a great deal of wind in anyone who eats too many too fast. Noah, who has recently learned the lesson of the chilli, makes a note to start with a very small portion.

Kofi shows Noah a drawing of a group of microbes called Bifidobacteria, which are known to grow well on fibres such as inulin and on the sugars in human milk. They are particularly common in the guts of babies, and many scientists regard them as friendly residents, although Kofi adds that being friendly depends on the situation and that scientists avoid simple labels. Noah says that he would very much like a plate of those on his side.

Noah sees an advertisement for a prebiotic powder that promises a perfect gut in two weeks and shows a smiling woman skipping across a field. Ines says that whole foods should come first, that the evidence for powders is mixed, and that a promise of perfection is itself a reason to be careful, since no honest scientist would ever make one. Noah decides to spend the money on lentils, which are cheaper and have never skipped across a field.

Ines adds a warning that some people with irritable bowel syndrome react badly to certain prebiotic fibres, which are found in onions, garlic, beans and many other healthy foods, because the fermentation produces gas and pain in a sensitive gut. Anyone in that situation should ask a doctor or registered dietitian for a plan, since cutting out whole groups of foods without help can be a mistake. Noah says that he is lucky to be able to eat onions, and she agrees that it is not something to take for granted.

Noah's older sister Mara visits on Sunday with her small son Leo, and she stops in the doorway of the flat with a look of complete disbelief. The kitchen smells of garlic, leeks and simmering soup, the fridge is covered in a chart, and the man who once lived on crisps is stirring a pot of vegetables as if he had done it all his life. She asks Ines, who has come round with a loaf, what exactly she has done to her brother.

Ines introduces resistant starch, a kind of starch that survives digestion in the small intestine and travels onward to feed the microbes in the large intestine, where it is fermented like fibre. Potatoes, rice and pasta that have been cooked and then cooled contain more of it than they do when they are hot, and so do slightly green bananas, oats and beans. Noah says that it is the first time he has ever heard that leftovers might be better than the original.

When cooked starch cools down, its structure changes into a more tightly packed form that digestive juices find harder to break down, which is why the cooled potato holds more resistant starch than the freshly boiled one. Reheating the food keeps at least some of the change, so a hot meal made from cooled leftovers still counts, although the exact amounts vary with the food and the method. Noah says that this is the first scientific reason he has found to cook too much on purpose.

Ines gives Noah an important safety rule about cooked rice, which is that it must be cooled quickly, ideally within an hour, then kept in the fridge and eaten within a day. Some bacteria in rice form spores that survive cooking, and if the rice is left warm on the counter they can multiply and make a person ill, so it is better to be strict about this than sorry. Noah writes the rule on a card in large letters and sticks it on the wall beside the kettle.

For Sunday lunch Noah makes a potato salad with the skins left on, boiled on Saturday, cooled quickly and kept in the fridge, and then mixed with fresh herbs, spring onions and a spoonful of plain yoghurt. Mara, who has come to the lunch expecting to be polite, is surprised by how good it is, and her small son Leo asks for a second helping and then, to everyone's astonishment, a third. Noah is delighted, and says that he has found his true vocation at last.

Polyphenols, Ines announces, are colourful substances found in many plants, such as purple cabbage, blueberries, green tea and dark chocolate. Gut microbes break many of them down into other substances that the body can absorb, and research on what these substances do is promising but still young, which means that nobody should make large claims. Noah says that the researchers appear to have found a very colourful and delicious subject.

Kofi boils some purple cabbage, pours the deep violet juice into three glasses and invites Noah to experiment, in a scene that looks like a children's party. A splash of lemon juice turns one of the glasses bright pink, and a pinch of baking soda turns another a surprising blue-green, which shows that the colours of plants are real chemicals that respond to their surroundings. Noah, delighted, drinks none of it, because Kofi has warned him that it tastes terrible.

Ines gives Noah a simple rule that is easy to follow at the shops, which is to put as many different colours as possible on the plate, from red peppers and orange carrots to green peas and purple cabbage. It is only a rough guide, because the colour of a food does not guarantee exactly what is inside it, but it helps a busy person to vary a meal without any counting. Noah makes a rainbow stir-fry and sends Tomasz a photograph, with the single word jealous.

Ines explains that tea, coffee, olive oil, cocoa, nuts and berries all contain polyphenols, which is good news for a man who drinks coffee at every red light. Moderate amounts are fine for most adults, though she adds that anyone who is pregnant or taking medicine should ask a doctor about caffeine, and that coffee is a pleasure and not a cure. Noah, who has been secretly dreading the day when she would ban his coffee, sighs with relief.

Noah asks hopefully about red wine, which is often said to be rich in helpful polyphenols, but Ines shakes her head. Alcohol is not a health food, she says, and it can harm the gut and the rest of the body. The polyphenols in wine are no reason to drink it, whereas grapes, berries and tea provide them without the risk, and Noah says that he asked only for scientific reasons, which she says she believes.

By the end of the week Noah's dinner plate looks like a painter's palette, with orange, green, purple and gold in careful stripes, and his plant count on the fridge has reached twenty-five. Tomasz says that he is beginning to look like a salad, but he secretly asks for the potato recipe on the following Monday, when he thinks that no one is listening. Noah smiles and writes it down for him, adding that it works best with the skins left on.

On Saturday Ines takes Noah to a stall at the street market that is crowded with glass jars in every shade of red, green and cream. Fermented foods such as yoghurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut and miso are made with the help of microbes, and many of them still contain living ones when they are eaten, some of which may help the gut. Noah feels as though he has wandered into the neighbourhood where his own microbes go shopping.

The stallholder is a cheerful woman called Dara, who makes her own kimchi and sauerkraut in a back room from cabbage, salt, garlic and a good deal of patience. She tells Noah that the microbes already living on the cabbage do most of the work, turning the sugars into acids that give the food its sharp, tangy taste and help to keep it from spoiling. Noah suspects that it is the first time that he has been given a lecture by a stallholder with such obvious joy.

Dara explains that not every food that is fermented still contains live microbes when it reaches the table. Bread is baked, many shop pickles are made with vinegar, and a good deal of sauerkraut is heat-treated, so a careful shopper looks for the words live, raw or unpasteurised on the label. Noah is relieved to discover that the best jars are kept in the cold section, which makes them easy to find.

Dara shows Noah a photograph of her kitchen, where rows of jars of kimchi sit patiently on the counter under clean cloths. The cabbage is mixed with salt, garlic, ginger and chilli, then packed down, and it bubbles gently for several days as the microbes ferment it and fill the air with a sharp, spicy smell. Noah, who is not a fan of spicy food, buys a small jar of the mildest variety to try at home.

Dara pours Noah a small cup of kefir, a tangy, slightly fizzy drink made by adding small grains full of microbes to milk and letting it stand for a day. It usually contains a wider mixture of microbes than ordinary yoghurt does, and there are also versions made from soya milk or water for those who avoid dairy. Noah drinks it with an expression of polite surprise, and then, to his astonishment, asks for another.

Back at the laboratory, Ines points to a chart of rising bars and tells Noah about a small university trial in which volunteers were asked to eat more fermented foods for ten weeks. At the end of that time, their gut microbes were more varied than they had been at the beginning, and some signs of inflammation in their blood had gone down. Noah says that it sounds like a scientific reason to go back to the market, and Ines says that it is a modest one.

Ines is careful to point out the limits of the trial, which was small and short and involved only a few dozen adults, so that no firm rules can be built on it. The results need to be repeated by other scientists, and what suits one person may not suit another, since every gut community begins from a different place. Noah says that he finds her caution reassuring, and she says that this is the nicest thing that anyone has said to her this year.

Ines reminds Noah that fermented vegetables such as sauerkraut and kimchi are made with a good deal of salt, which is part of what keeps them safe. People who have been told to limit their salt intake, for example because of high blood pressure, should check the label and ask their doctor before eating them in large amounts. Noah, who rarely worries about salt, reads the numbers on his jar for the first time.

Dara sells Noah a tub of miso, a rich, salty paste made from fermented soya beans, and shows him how to dissolve a spoonful in a little warm water. At home he stirs it into a soup of tofu, spring onions and greens after the heat has been switched off, because boiling water can kill the live microbes and spoil the delicate flavour. It is the quickest and most comforting dinner of his week, and he wonders why he waited so long.

Noah decides to start small, with a spoonful of kimchi, a bowl of live yoghurt or a little glass of kefir every day, and to see how his stomach feels. Ines advises anyone who has a weak immune system, or who is pregnant, to ask a doctor before eating foods that are unpasteurised, since a careful choice matters more than enthusiasm. Noah notes it all in his book, and nods when she says that a little every day beats a lot once.

Probiotic pills and drinks contain particular living microbes, and Ines explains that the evidence for them is mixed, since some strains help with certain conditions but others do little at all. The microbes usually do not stay for long after a person stops taking them, and they are no replacement for a varied diet. Anyone who is tempted to buy one for a particular problem should ask a doctor or registered dietitian first, so Noah puts the bottle back on the pharmacy shelf.

Ines points to the label of a probiotic bottle, where a long Latin name is followed by a short code of letters and numbers, and she explains that the code identifies the exact strain. Scientists define a probiotic as a live microbe that gives a health benefit in the right amount. The benefit belongs to the particular strain, so one that helps with a problem may do nothing for another, and Noah says that it is like hiring someone by looking only at their surname.

Ines says, in fairness to the pills, that some strains have been shown in careful trials to help with certain problems, such as diarrhoea after a course of antibiotics. The results differ from one product to the next and from one study to another, and none of them amounts to a miracle, so the sensible way to see a probiotic is as a medicine-like product with a narrow use. Noah says that it is a relief to hear a fair account of both sides.

Ines warns that probiotics are not harmless for everyone, since live microbes can occasionally cause serious infections in people whose defences are weak. Anyone with a weakened immune system or a serious illness, and the parents of very premature babies, should take medical advice before using them, and the same goes for anyone who is unsure. Noah, who had been picturing probiotics as a type of friendly sweet, writes the word careful next to his notes.

Ines tells Noah that in many countries supplements are not tested and approved in the same strict way as medicines, so the quality of a product can vary a good deal. The number of live microbes promised on the label may not match what is actually inside the capsule, especially near the end of its shelf life, and a pharmacist can help a person to choose with care. Noah picks up a bottle, reads the label and puts it back for the second time that day.

Ines draws three boxes on a paper napkin to help Noah to keep the long words straight, because he has been mixing them up for a week. Probiotics are the live microbes, prebiotics are the fibres that feed them, and postbiotics are the useful substances that the microbes make, such as the short-chain fatty acids that he has met already. Noah takes the napkin home, folds it carefully and slips it into his notebook like a treasure map.

Ines shows Noah an advertisement for a seven-day gut detox, complete with dramatic before-and-after photographs and a banner promising to cure almost everything. She teaches him the warning signs of a weak claim, which are that no strain or ingredient is named, that no trial is mentioned and that the language of fear and miracles is used to hurry the buyer along. Noah says that he can see these signs in half the advertisements on his tram.

Noah decides to make his own sauerkraut, following a recipe that Dara has written on the back of a receipt. He washes the jar and his hands with great care, slices a cabbage thinly, rubs it with salt and presses it down firmly until its own juice rises above the leaves and covers them. Ines, watching from the doorway, says that the most important ingredients are cleanliness and patience.

By the third day the jar is full of tiny bubbles that rise slowly through the cabbage, and the whole kitchen smells pleasantly sour, as the microbes go about their work. Noah checks every morning that the leaves stay under the brine, because anything that rises to the surface is exposed to the air, and he presses it down gently with a clean spoon. It feels like looking after a tiny and extremely quiet pet that lives in a jar.

After ten days of watching, Noah opens the jar and smells it carefully, with Ines and Kofi leaning in beside him. A clean, sour smell is normal, Ines says, but fuzzy mould or a smell like something rotten means that the whole jar must be thrown away, and when in doubt, the rule is always to throw it out. Noah finds that the smell is mild and pleasant, and the first forkful of cabbage is crisp, tangy and a little bit salty, and he is almost ridiculously proud.

Mara has a bad chest infection that will not go away, and her doctor gives her a course of antibiotics after listening carefully to her breathing. After weeks of hearing Noah talk about the gut, she telephones him in a worried voice and asks whether she should refuse them, which is the sort of question that makes him feel suddenly responsible. He promises to ask Ines before he says anything that he might later regret, and he runs next door at once.

Ines tells Noah to say one thing clearly to his sister, which is that antibiotics have saved countless lives and that nobody should refuse a prescribed medicine because of what they have read about the gut. It is true that antibiotics also disturb the gut microbes, which is one reason why they should be taken only when a doctor prescribes them, and exactly as the instructions say. Noah repeats the message to Mara over the telephone that evening, and he hears her breathe out in relief.

Ines explains that antibiotics work against bacteria and not against viruses, which means that they do nothing for a cold or for flu, however miserable the patient may feel. Taking them when they are not needed disturbs the gut microbes for no benefit and also helps resistant bacteria to spread, which makes future infections harder to treat, so a doctor's judgement matters. Noah thinks of every time that he has demanded a tablet for a cough, and winces.

Ines says that after a course of antibiotics the community of gut microbes usually begins to recover over the following weeks and months, although for some people a few changes may last longer. Scientists are still studying why the recovery is faster in some people than in others, and how much it matters for health in the long run, so the honest answer to many questions is that nobody knows yet. Noah is quietly glad that she says it so plainly, because it makes the rest of her advice easier to believe.

Some people develop loose stools while they take antibiotics or soon afterwards, and in most cases it is mild and passes by itself. If it is severe, if it contains blood, or if it comes with a fever or strong stomach pain, the person should speak to a doctor quickly, because a harmful germ can sometimes take advantage of the disturbed gut. Noah writes this down in capital letters and passes it on to Mara by message.

Noah cooks a gentle vegetable soup with carrots, potatoes and a little rice, and carries it across the city to Mara's flat with a banana and a tub of plain yoghurt. She is tired and weak and has no appetite to speak of, but she eats half the bowl and says that it is the nicest thing that anyone has brought her all week. Leo asks whether it is the same soup that makes Uncle Noah laugh, and nobody knows what he means.

Ines stops in an aisle of brightly coloured packets and explains what scientists mean by the phrase ultra-processed food, which is food made largely from industrial ingredients and additives that are not found in a home kitchen. Biscuits, sweet cereals, many ready meals and fizzy drinks are typical examples, and as a group they tend to be low in fibre and high in sugar, salt or fat. Noah looks down at his own basket and realises, with a small pang of guilt, how many of the packets he knows.

Ines says that some additives, such as the emulsifiers that stop oil and water from separating in a food, have changed the gut microbes of animals in laboratory studies. The evidence in people is limited and mixed, and the studies are hard to carry out, so nobody can say yet how much it matters or which products might be the problem. Noah finds it oddly refreshing that she does not exaggerate in either direction, whether to frighten him or to please him.

Ines says that diets high in sugar and fat and low in fibre are linked with a less varied set of gut microbes, and that the link has been found in several different studies. It is not settled how much of the effect comes from the sugar and fat themselves and how much from the missing plants, and it certainly does not prove that a single slice of cake does any harm. Noah says that he is very glad to hear it, and he orders a large slice of cake.

Noah and Tomasz sit on a bench beside their bicycles and share a large slice of chocolate cake, and Noah finds, to his surprise, that he enjoys it without a trace of guilt. Ines had told him that no single food is a villain, that a few treats are part of normal life, and that a calm relationship with food matters as much as any quantity of fibre. Tomasz says that this is the best advice that he has ever heard, and takes the last bite with a smile.

Ines tells Noah that poor sleep and high stress both seem to affect the gut, and that the gut in return seems to influence sleep and stress, so that the effects can travel round in a circle. Most of the evidence is still early, and a good deal of it comes from animals, but the connections are plausible enough to be taken seriously. Noah says that he has just been given a good reason to go to bed on time.

Noah's working day is uneven, with early starts, late finishes and meals eaten at whatever hour the parcels allow, and he mentions that he often eats at midnight after a long shift. Ines says that irregular sleep and mealtimes may disturb the body's daily rhythms, including those of the gut, and gut microbes themselves seem to follow a daily cycle, although most of this research is early. Noah decides to try to eat at roughly the same times each day, even if the parcels object.

Ines advises Noah to avoid a heavy meal just before bed, since lying down soon after eating can let stomach acid creep upward and cause heartburn. Eating earlier in the evening helps many people, but if heartburn happens often or wakes a person at night, it should be discussed with a doctor and not simply treated with tablets from the shop. Noah, who has ignored such feelings for months, writes a note to himself to book an appointment.

Ines suggests that Noah use his red lights for something other than eating, and teaches him a slow breathing exercise that he can practise on the saddle. He breathes in gently for a count of four and out for a count of six, and finds that the busy city seems quieter and the lights seem to change faster. She is careful to say that this will not cure anything, but that calm is useful in itself.

Ines, who has persuaded Noah to let her jog beside his bicycle on a Sunday hill, says between breaths that regular exercise is linked with a more varied gut community and with more regular bowel movements. Most of the studies are small, and they cannot show that exercise is the only cause, but the link has been found by more than one team of researchers. Noah, who is not even breathing hard, says that he is clearly in excellent condition.

Noah is already extremely active, and Ines points out that, for him, the question is not how to move more but how to eat and drink enough to fuel a long day on the road. Fibre-rich foods are filling and can leave a person feeling full on fewer calories, so she asks him to be sure that he does not eat too little, adding snacks and a larger breakfast if he needs them. Noah, who had worried about being too greedy, is happy to follow this advice.

Fibre soaks up water as it moves through the gut, and it works best when a person drinks enough fluid, since a lack of water, fibre and movement is a common cause of constipation. Drinking regularly through the day is a simple habit, and Noah, who spends his working hours on a bicycle in the sun, notices that he often forgets to drink anything at all until the evening. He fills a bottle, fastens it firmly to the frame of his bicycle and resolves to sip at every red light.

Ines mentions other things that can help with constipation, such as not ignoring the urge to go, keeping a calm routine and, for some people, using a small footstool, although the evidence for it is modest. Some medicines can also cause constipation, so a person who is unsure about their own tablets should ask a pharmacist or doctor instead of simply stopping them. Noah, who had never discussed the subject so openly, finds that it is not as embarrassing as he feared.

Ines says that healthy bowel habits vary a great deal from one person to the next, from several times a day to a few times a week. What matters is what is normal for each person, she adds, and any lasting change from that pattern, especially with pain, blood or weight loss, should be mentioned to a doctor. Noah realises that he has never once paid attention to his own pattern and decides that it is time to start.

Ines draws a circle on the whiteboard with a tiny gut in the middle and five words arranged around it, which are plants, water, movement, sleep and calm. She says that none of them works alone, and that the order matters less than the habit of coming back to them every day, in small and ordinary ways. Noah takes a photograph of the circle and makes it the background of his phone.

Ines becomes unusually serious, and tells Noah to write down a list of warning signs in a different colour from everything else in his notebook. A person should see a doctor, and not a diet book, for blood in the stool, black stools, unexplained weight loss, ongoing pain or a lasting change in bowel habits. Noah copies the list in red, underlines it twice and says that he does not intend to forget a word of it.

Ines explains that these warning signs can have many different causes, most of which can be treated, and that she has no wish to frighten Noah or anyone else. Checking early is much better than waiting and hoping, and it is never a waste of a doctor's time, because doctors would rather see a hundred people with harmless problems than miss one with a serious one. Noah says that he has been in the habit of ignoring his body, and she says that it is time to stop.

Ines mentions that many countries invite adults above a certain age to take part in bowel screening, usually with a simple test that can be done at home and posted away. She says that people should accept the invitation when it arrives, because the test can find problems early, sometimes before any symptoms appear, and that no diet, however good, can replace it. Noah thinks of his parents, who are old enough to receive the letter, and decides to call them that night.

Tomasz, who has been unusually quiet for a week, tells Noah that he has noticed blood on several occasions and has been too embarrassed to see a doctor. Noah remembers the list that he wrote in red, and he sits beside his friend while Tomasz telephones the clinic and, after a long pause, books an appointment for the following morning. Tomasz says that he is grateful, but that Noah is not allowed to mention it to the others at the office.

Tomasz sees Dr Ellis the next morning, and she listens carefully, examines him politely and arranges a few tests, explaining each step as she goes. Within a couple of weeks she finds a cause that can be treated, and she tells him firmly that he was right to come and that waiting would only have made things worse. Tomasz tells Noah about it in a whisper outside the office, and Noah feels a deep and quiet relief.

Ines introduces Noah to her friend Hana, a registered dietitian who works at a community clinic and who spends her days helping people to eat comfortably. Hana explains that some people with bowel conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome, need a personal plan that is based on their own symptoms, and that general advice from a book is not a substitute. Noah listens with great respect, since she is the first real expert he has met who is not a scientist.

Hana explains that for some people with irritable bowel syndrome a dietitian may guide them through a short and temporary diet called low FODMAP, which limits certain fermentable carbohydrates. It has three steps, which are to cut back, to bring foods back one at a time and to personalise the result. It is not meant to last for life, because a long restriction can starve the microbes that a person is trying to keep, and Noah finally understands why Ines worries about people who cut out foods alone.

Hana gives Noah a warning that he has heard nowhere else, which is that anyone who suspects coeliac disease should be tested before they stop eating gluten. If the person cuts it out first, the tests may wrongly seem normal, and a real condition could go unnoticed and untreated, so the correct first step is always to see a doctor. Noah says that he has a friend who is about to start a gluten-free diet purely because it sounds modern.

Noah is tempted by an advertisement for a cleanse drink and a postal stool test that promises a personal diet plan, and he mentions it to Hana with a mixture of hope and guilt. She says that the evidence for such products is weak, that the body already clears its own waste through the liver, kidneys and gut, and that some detox teas contain strong laxatives that can do harm. Noah closes the advertisement, deletes the page and, to his surprise, feels oddly lighter.

Ines reminds Noah that a baby's microbes begin to form at birth, and that the diet of a baby or a small child should always follow the advice of a doctor or health visitor. Small children also need a balanced diet, because too much fibre can fill them up before they have eaten enough energy, and the same caution applies to pregnancy, to people on medicine and to anyone with a long-term condition. Noah makes a list of all of them in his notebook, and writes ask first at the top.

Noah's new breakfast is a bowl of warm porridge made with oats, topped with a spoonful of mixed seeds, a handful of berries and a dollop of plain live yoghurt. It takes five minutes to make, costs very little and keeps him comfortably full until the middle of the morning, when he used to be hunting for a pastry. He counts at least five different plants in the bowl and writes the number proudly on the fridge.

For his lunch box, Noah mixes cold brown rice with tinned mixed beans, chopped carrots, spring onions and fresh herbs, and he dresses it with olive oil and lemon. It is cheap and easy to carry in a bicycle bag, and the cooked and cooled rice adds resistant starch to the fibre of the beans and vegetables. He eats it on a park bench and, for once, he does not feel sleepy afterwards.

Because the weather is getting warm, Noah buys a small insulated bag and a freezer block, and he packs his lunch box between them each morning. Ines reminds him that rice, cooked beans and other prepared foods should not sit out in the heat for hours, since harmful bacteria multiply quickly in warm food, and that the cool bag is an important part of the plan. Noah says that it is the first time he has ever felt like a professional.

For dinner on Wednesday, Noah cooks a large stew of brown lentils, carrots, celery, onions and garlic, while Ines stands beside him tasting from a wooden spoon and offering suggestions that he politely ignores. The onions and garlic provide prebiotic fibres, the lentils provide protein and plenty of fibre, and the whole pot costs hardly anything and makes four generous portions. They eat at the little table and agree that it is the best meal of the week so far.

Noah makes a list of the snacks that can survive a day in a bicycle bag without turning into a disaster, and it includes fruit, a small bag of nuts, a boiled egg and a thick slice of wholemeal bread. The egg lives in the cool bag, the nuts in a pocket and the banana in the basket, and he stops at the fruit stall on his round each afternoon to choose something fresh. The stallholder has begun to call him the banana man, and he is surprisingly pleased about it.

Noah goes out for lunch with Tomasz and studies the menu of a busy street cafe with the seriousness of a man who is reading a map. He chooses a dish with beans and roasted vegetables, adds a side salad and asks for wholemeal bread, and he discovers that eating out can be friendly to the gut without being dull. Tomasz, who orders chips, looks at his plate and then, a little embarrassed, reaches for the salad.

At the sandwich shop where he once bought a white roll every day, Noah asks for a wholemeal one filled with hummus, plenty of salad and a little cheese. It is not a perfect lunch and he does not pretend that it is, but it contains far more fibre and variety than the plain ham roll that he once ate without thinking. The woman behind the counter says that she has noticed a change in him, and he says that so has he.

On a quiet Sunday Noah cooks a large pot of bean and vegetable stew, divides it into labelled containers and cools them quickly in a basin of cold water. He puts most of them straight into the freezer, where they will keep for weeks, and Ines reminds him that anything that is reheated must be piping hot all the way through before it is eaten. Noah feels like a man with a bank account, except that this one is made of beans.

Mara has recovered from her illness, and she comes to cook with Noah on Sunday while Leo watches from a chair with a serious expression. She has started to hide red lentils in her tomato sauce, where they melt into the sauce without a trace, and Leo eats his apple with the skin on, to the loud astonishment of his mother. Noah says that the child is clearly a natural, and Mara says that the child is clearly a fan of Uncle Noah.

At the end of the week Noah counts thirty different plants, adds them up three times to be sure and writes the number in large letters on the office whiteboard, to the cheers of Tomasz and Pavel. Ines, who has been invited to see it, congratulates him warmly but reminds him that thirty is a marker and not a prize, and that the real result is the habit, which now seems to be his. Noah says that he has never been so happy to be told that he has not won anything.

Noah sits down with his shopping receipts at the end of the month and finds, to his considerable surprise, that he has spent less on food than he did before the project began. Dried beans, oats, frozen vegetables, cabbage and carrots cost very little, they fill the stomach and they keep well, whereas the crisps and pastries of his old life had been small and expensive disappointments. Ines says that gut-friendly food has always been the food of people who had to be careful with money.

After six weeks Noah knocks on Ines's door with his bicycle beside him and tells her, with a wide and slightly foolish smile, that he feels lighter and has more energy in the afternoons. She is delighted for him, but she reminds him gently that everybody's results will differ and that a feeling, however welcome, is not proof of anything. Noah says that he knows, and that he is happy to have a feeling anyway.

Ines writes a list of possible reasons on the whiteboard, as honest scientists should, and Noah reads it with a mixture of respect and frustration. The extra fibre may have helped, but so may the smaller number of crisps, the more regular sleep, the warmer weather and the simple fact that Noah has been paying attention to himself for the first time in years. She says that one person's story can never tell the cause apart from the coincidence.

Noah turns slowly through the pages of his green notebook and sees some clear patterns emerge from the charts and the little drawn faces. There are fewer afternoon dips, a calmer stomach and a gentler daily rhythm than at the start, although Ines reminds him once more that a diary can only show patterns and cannot prove what caused them. He finds the first page, with its crooked question about lunch, and decides that he would like to answer it properly.

Ines stands at the whiteboard, which is now covered with question marks clustered around a drawing of the gut, and she says that this is the most important picture of the whole six weeks. Much about the microbiome is still unknown, including what a healthy one looks like and why people respond so differently to the same food. Good science means being willing to admit what we do not know, and Noah says that this is why he trusted her from the start.

Ines tells Noah that the unknowns are exactly what make the field exciting, because most of the serious research on the gut microbiome is only a few decades old. Careful trials are now under way in many countries, and honest scientists keep asking better questions, which is slower than selling a miracle but far more likely to be right in the end. Kofi, who has been listening from the doorway, says quietly that he chose this field precisely because of the question marks.

Ines gives Noah five questions to ask whenever he reads a headline about food and health, and she writes them on the whiteboard in her neatest handwriting. Was the study done on people or on animals, how large was it, did it show a link or a proper trial, has anyone repeated it, and is somebody trying to sell something at the end? Noah copies them into his notebook, and he tries them out on a newspaper article that evening, and the article does not survive.

Noah decides how he will carry the new habits forward when the six weeks are over, and he writes them in his notebook as three short promises. He will keep adding plants slowly, drink water and sleep as well as the parcels allow, and ask a doctor whenever something seems wrong instead of hoping that it goes away. He signs the page with a flourish, as if it were an important contract.

To celebrate the end of the six weeks, Noah gives a thirty-plant dinner in his tiny flat, and every guest is asked to bring a different plant. Ines, Kofi, Tomasz, Pavel and Mara fill the table with salads, bean stews, roasted roots, fruit and a jar of home-made sauerkraut, and Leo brings an apple, which he insists must be counted. They raise their glasses of kefir to the microbes, and Tomasz says that it is the strangest toast of his life.

The next evening, Noah and Ines sit on a bench with a bicycle between them and agree that feeding the gut is mostly a matter of eating more plants, and more kinds of plants. This book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with a health condition, an allergy, a pregnancy, a child to feed or a medicine to take should ask a doctor or registered dietitian first. For everyone else, the next step is small and friendly, which is to add one new plant to tomorrow's meal.
